#5449. What happened to Helen Haines seemed unthinkable. It's a warning we can't ignore

How do we comprehend this savagery against someone so conscientious and unifying?

Especially if it becomes contextualised in an otherwise "valid" politics of division and anger.

The sheer incomprehensibility shocks us into an overdue awakening.

Jarringly, we learn that threats of rape and murder against our elected representatives are endemic, and that there are people among us who act this way.

These are anti-democrats, morally adrift, politically deracinated, dangerous. Are they new or were they always there?

The Minister for Multicultural Affairs Anne Aly reports 19 death threats in the past week alone.

Someone laments via social media on Monday, (that is, before the attack on Helen Haines) that "not enough politicians are afraid for their lives right now," reports Nine's Jacqueline Maley.

Another aggressor observes, in the hours after, that Senator Jacqui Lambie - the subject of a vile One Nation attack - needs to meet a LandCruiser, reports Tanya Plibersek.

Every MP and senator experiences this, but women are vastly more targeted. This is a technologically enabled misogyny, a terrorism where hatred meets impulse. But who would do such a thing? Surely nobody we know, right?

We assume we are all equally appalled but cannot now unknow that some feel differently.

Our social democratic settlement is listing, beset by a variety of forces, not least of which is that we stopped strengthening it decades ago.

Renovation is urgent. Our leaders behaved as if democracy was a self-expressing, self-renewing, self-legitimising machine. That it was girded by rules, fixed players, agreed norms, even as their parties gamed it to death by ignoring safe seat voters - their own and their opponents'.

The key to the whole thing was that voters recognised the legitimacy of the government even if personally they had not voted for it.

Now, in the face of pernicious new inputs like foreign-controlled social media, the social licence for a responsive form of legitimate government is being withdrawn.

Violence and the spectre of it looms. Australia is not a country of brutality-worship like the US. We haven't elevated gun ownership over life itself, and we don't stage blood-sports on the lawns of The Lodge.

We are better but we cannot be complacent.

As academics, Bongiorno and Black observed this week, "democracy is a practice as much as a system". Its defence requires more than trite praise for the Australian marvel of compulsory preferential voting and an independent electoral commission. It must be lived, animated, taught, practised.

There are multiple worthy options including genuine national civics education, deliberative assemblies and citizens juries on contentious issues, fixed four-year federal terms, and optional 16- to 18-year-old voting.

Meanwhile, the public square has surrendered to pitched battle, vaulting incivility. Harsh words eclipse reasoned argument.

Even those of us in the communicating business experience a gnawing impotence - the harder we try, the more our invocations fall short.

Grasping for clues, a weak consensus forms behind Anthony Albanese's vague entreaty - and that of ASIO boss Mike Burgess - to "lower the temperature". It seems right, this proposition that the febrile tone of public discourse had been, if not causal, then in some way facilitative.

But what does it mean and how is it achieved?

Nobody knows. This, like all the other attempts at finger-pointing leads us everywhere and nowhere.

Situating this vile incident within the zeitgeist invites this categorisation dilemma - a confusion of specific-versus-general illuminating nothing.

Critically, the deranged impetus of Wangaratta remains unclear. Is it political extremism, a family property dispute or a mental health episode? It's as if these cannot co-exist or unduly magnify each other.

That the normalisation of aggression and abuse in political dealings may itself be another symptom is acknowledged but left largely uninterrogated. Partly, because it is unprovable.

While the criminal justice system begins a tightly defined prosecution, the ailing political system, its lower evidentiary standards already satisfied, ponders a wider soul-searching.

But where to start? The antisocial wilds of social media? Parliamentary raucousness and the daily disrespect emanating from Capital Hill? Or mainstream media cynicism and the vomitus indignations of partisan foghorns for whom outrage is bankable.

What is clear is that in what was the world's model liberal democracy, the case against a negligent political class seems strong.

Ignoring this, we comfort ourselves with terms like turning point, wake-up call, watershed, and make well-intentioned predictions about the longer-term implications of this terrible moment.

Experience tells a less optimistic story. Britain's political class was rocked by the stabbing murder of Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016 and vowed to lift its standards, be kinder, behave more responsibly.

Like Tony Abbott's "kinder gentler polity", these fine intentions were quickly forgotten. Two more political figures have been killed since.

Kim Leadbeater, the sister of the late Jo Cox is now herself an MP. Speaking on Australian media this week she noted a certain repetitive theme when attacks occur.

Politicians and media proprietors commit to a more respectful, less personalised comportment. And to be fair, most mean it.

But as Leadbeater told Sarah Ferguson, while the families and friends carry the trauma in their hearts and recall it every day, the rest of us go back to our own lives, to new problems and, regrettably, old habits.

#5450. Die Besitzenden von heute und die Mitmenschlichkeit: Ein Essay zur Lage von Peter Rosei

Wie sieht Reichsein heute aus? Gibt es ein ethisches Fundament, wie noch bei Calvin, nach dem Reichtum weniger ein Luxus, vielmehr eine soziale Aufgabe ist?

Money, money, money! Der Markt verschafft jedem, der Geld hat, ohne Unterschied das Gefühl, wer zu sein – im Bezahlvorgang akzentuiert sich das, je nach Kasse freilich, mit großem oder kleinem Impact.

Im Gegensatz zu den Besitzenden des 19. und wohl auch der ersten Hälfte des 20. Jahrhunderts, die im Großen und Ganzen, bei großbürgerlicher Repräsentation, vom puritanischen Ethos des Sparens geprägt waren – um mit dem so Ersparten umso mehr in ihre jeweiligen Projekte investieren zu können, oder weitverbreitet, sich in sozialen, künstlerischen oder kulturellen Projekten zu verewigen, sehen wir bei den Besitzenden von heute einen Hang zur Selbstdarstellung. Zum Beispiel in Unternehmungen wie etwa der Förderung von Autorennen oder Fußballklubs, Sponsoring von Extremsportlern und Ähnlichem, die eher im Feld oder Vorfeld der Werbung für die von ihnen erzeugten Produkte zu verorten sind.

#5451. First international flight takes off from new Sydney airport

Western Sydney International Airport offers the first alternative to the city's main airport, which has been operating for more than a century.

An Air New Zealand plane takes off as the first international flight to depart the newly-opened Western Sydney International Airport in Sydney on Oct 26, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Saeed Khan)

SYDNEY: The first international flight took off on Monday (Oct 26) from a new, multi-billion-dollar airport in the fast-growing western suburbs of Sydney.

After more than four decades of planning, Western Sydney International Airport offers the first alternative to the city's main airport, which has been operating for more than a century.

An Air New Zealand plane from Auckland landed and soon afterwards flew out of the airport in the morning, launching a three-flights-a-week service to Sydney's largely working-class western suburbs.

"It's not every day you get to be part of opening a brand-new international airport," said Air New Zealand chief operations officer Kate Boyer.

"Western Sydney is home to more than 2.5 million people and it's a further gateway for Australian visitors to discover everything our country has to offer."

The new single-runway airport, Australia's first new major aviation hub in more than five decades, began domestic flights on Sunday, and freight operations in July.

Sydney's main airport, Kingsford Smith, is Australia's busiest, its three runways handling more than 42 million passengers last year.

Lying in Botany Bay just 9km from the city centre, planes using the airport roar over many city homes, and a curfew bars passenger aircraft from operating during the night.

The new airport in western Sydney has no such restrictions.

"Through our 24-hour operations, Western Sydney International Airport gives airlines greater flexibility to connect into global hubs and travellers more choice in how they reach the world," said airport chief executive Simon Hickey.

Qantas' budget carrier Jetstar is now the main domestic carrier, flying to the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane.

The airport says other international carriers are coming, including Qatar Airways from December 2027, Fiji Airways from March 2027, and Vietjet Air from January 2027.

Built at a cost of A$5.3 billion (US$3.7 billion), excluding surrounding transport works, the airport is reachable by road but is not expected to have a direct rail link until at least December 2027.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the new airport marked a "wonderful new chapter" for Australia.

It would also drive economic and jobs into western Sydney, an area often overshadowed by the city's famed harbour and central business district (CBD), he said at the weekend.

"For too long, Sydney has looked towards the harbour and the CBD. What this does is turn it around to where people live, to where jobs occur, to where investment occurs in western Sydney."

#5454. 'A little more unique': Wrong design accidentally added to Sydney Marathon medal

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

Organisers of the 2026 Sydney Marathon have been left red-faced after unveiling a finishers’ medal featuring a stadium in Germany — thousands of kilometres from the race finish line.

The two-sided medal features Sydney landmarks, including the Opera House and Sydney Harbour Bridge, but also depicts the distinctive Allianz Arena in Munich.

Marathon organisers have acknowledged the "unfortunate error", with the medal showing the German stadium’s distinctive diamond-patterned exterior rather than the flatter design of Sydney’s Allianz Stadium.

"A little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finishers' medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.

"We're not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error, though it's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour."

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

The medal's reception on social media was light-hearted.

"Oh, dear. Oh, this is bad," said Instagram account @morningcoffeerun, speculating that someone may have mixed up the stadiums in an online search for Allianz.

Munich's Allianz Arena treated the medal muddle with good humour.

"Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!" it posted on Instagram.

"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena — Sydney Opera — Unique Architecture — Both are worth a visit!"

The reverse side of the Sydney Marathon medal features a widely praised blue-and-gold design by Indigenous artist Ambrose Killian, who told the Agence-France Presse news agency that he was not involved in creating the Sydney skyline design.

"My artwork and creative contribution to this year's medal was specifically for the lanyard and the front side of the medal only," he said.

"I had no involvement in the design or production of the reverse side of the medal, including the incorrect inclusion of Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney.

"I take my work very seriously and would like to reiterate that my artwork story, importance and originality remains."

Marathon organisers say they expect a record number of more than 40,000 participants this year, each of whom will earn the medal as a "badge of honour" for completing the 42.2-kilometre course.

"With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive," the Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.

"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget," the spokesperson added.

"It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

#5456. Sparks will fly when Bulldog Butters returns to Adelaide for Gather Round

Updated October 26, 2026 — 4:01pm,first published 12:59pm

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Zak Butters will be bracing a fiery reception when he returns to Adelaide to play against the Power for the first time when the Western Bulldogs help draw a curtain on next year’s Gather Round.

The clash between Port Adelaide and Butters’ new club is the ninth game of the Gather Round fixture released by the AFL on Monday, and even has South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas – an avid Power fan – fired up.

Revered at the Power after three best and fairest awards and three All-Australian guernseys from 156 games, Butters officially became a Bulldog earlier this month, signing the richest contract in AFL history.

He stands to earn at least $17 million over the next nine years after crossing to the Dogs as a restricted free agent, aided by a complex side deal that convinced Port not to match the deal.

Raised near Bacchus Marsh as a Bulldogs supporter, Butters’ future was the subject of conjecture throughout the 2026 season, with the Dogs pipping Geelong for his coveted signature.

It’s not yet clear, how Port’s passionate fan base will respond to Butters, but the AFL have capitalised on the appeal of his clash with his former teammates by making it a marquee match of Gather Round.

It is one of three blockbuster games the league has scheduled at the Adelaide Oval to underpin the South Australian-based round - round four of the 2027 season.

The festivities will open on Thursday April 8, with the Crows seeking revenge for their semi-final loss in 2026 to the Brisbane Lions, and close four days later with Butters facing his former side.

In between, the league has scheduled a humdinger of a Saturday-night match between leading premiership fancies Fremantle and Hawthorn.

There are two other games scheduled at the Adelaide Oval across the weekend – Sydney v Collingwood on the Friday night and an early Saturday game between Carlton and Melbourne, who met in a wildcard final in 2026.

Gold Coast, GWS, Geelong and St Kilda are the four teams heading to the Barossa for their Gather Round games, while Richmond, West Coast, Essendon and North Melbourne are bound for Norwood Oval.

Malinauskas – an avid Power fan – was quick to spruik the Gather Round program, which coincides with the Easter school holidays, and the inclusion of a players’ parade on the Friday.

“The blockbuster weekend of footy will be boosted with the inaugural Players Parade on Friday, allowing fans to see their heroes from all 18 clubs in one spot,” he said.

“Personally, I’m looking forward to being at a packed Adelaide Oval to see Zak Butters take on his former teammates.”

Melbourne captain Max Gawn has applauded the club’s “brutal” list-management calls which led to the departure of favourite son Jack Viney, but hopes he can finish his career as a one-club player.

Gawn is off contract in 2027, but at 33 is still playing some of the best football of his career, which he attributes, in part, to his punishing off-season cycling regime.

The 2021 premiership skipper won All-Australian selection for the ninth time in 2026, and is keen to remain a Demon for life when contract discussions open. However, he understands the business of football, having watched his fellow premiership on-ball brigade of Clayton Oliver, Christian Petracca and Viney, along with key defender Steven May, depart over the past two seasons.

“I’m pretty keen in Melbourne. I understand ‘Vines’ would have said the same thing 12 months ago. So, I’ve just applauded ‘Lamby’ [list boss Tim Lamb] and King [coach Steven King], and if I’m the one that has to move on next year, and I still think there’s footy ahead of me, then that conversation will come, but right now, it does look like my finish will be with the Demons,” Gawn said on Monday.

However, speaking as an ambassador at the launch of the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, Gawn hinted he would be open to offers, should negotiations with the Demons not go as planned, and if new club Tasmania came calling.

“I mean, my phone’s always open,” Gawn said.

“I mean, I’m keen to jump in the commentary box with ‘Kino’ [SBS commentator Matt Keenan] and commentate the Tour de France at some point as well. So if SBS want to jump into my phone … but, no, I’m pretty keen to finish up in Melbourne.”

Viney, 32, managed only one game this season because of Achilles and back injuries, and struggled when recalled for the wildcard final against Carlton, the Demons losing by 19 points. He was given the option to explore opportunities elsewhere, or face the possibility of long spells in the VFL.

Viney and fellow Demon Trent Rivers were traded to West Coast on the final day of the trade period.

“I applaud the list management team; they’ve made some brutal decisions,” Gawn said.

“None more brutal than probably Jack this year, but you’ve seen with what we’re able to do this year, with most people tipping us [to finish] bottom four, and we come out and play some pretty good footy.”

Gawn said he was delighted that Essendon and the Eagles showed interest in Viney, his former co-captain.

“I went from a little bit of surprise [at his departure], and then I went a little bit of other clubs were making him feel generally loved,” Gawn said.

“And now, he’s like, once it got to a point where West Coast were interested, he’s like: ‘I want to get there so bad, I want to rejuvenate my career, I want to take my family over there’. So I’m really excited for him.”

Gawn said the Demons had needed a substantial make-over, having seen how quickly Geelong transformed, even after winning the 2022 premiership. Only nine Demons players now remain from the 2021 premiership team.

“I sat there and looked at that [2022 Geelong] team, I was like, OK, and then they play in the grand final three years later, and they had 10 or 15 new players in that team. And, at the same time, Melbourne was still running the round with the ’21 premiership team,” Gawn said.

“It’s like, well, we haven’t changed or adapted or moved on. We’re still trying to win it again with the ’21 premiership team, and Geelong, at that very same time, had changed over 15 players. It’s like, OK, this is what’s needed in a way to stay in the modern game.”

A cycling enthusiast who now has his own podcast on the sport, Gawn’s pre-season training program has so far included “Everesting” South Australia’s exhausting Willunga Hill, riding the 3.7km climb 39.5 times in 21 hours, and another punishing ride on the island of Phuket in Thailand. He will soon head to Patagonia, at the southern end of South America, to ride in the wilderness. This program will also include running.

After coaching Essendon through the second half of 2026, Dean Solomon will return to Gold Coast as an assistant coach to Damien Hardwick.

Solomon, now 46, was on the coaching staff at the Suns from the club’s inception in the AFL in 2011 to 2020, even serving three games as interim coach following the departure of Rodney Eade in 2017.

Solomon later joined the board at Essendon – the club where he made his name as a player and was part of the 2000 premiership team – but relinquished that position a year ago to return to a hands-on coaching role.

He started the 2026 season as an assistant to Brad Scott, and became the club’s stop-gap coach when Scott was sacked mid-season. Despite holding some ambition to become the senior coach permanently, Solomon’s hopes were dented by a record of just one win from his 12 games in charge.

After hiring Solomon’s former teammate Mark McVeigh as senior coach for 2027, Essendon announced last month that Solomon had declined their offer of another role in the football department and would return to live in NSW with his wife and children.

On Monday, the Suns spruiked Solomon’s recruitment as a homecoming.

“Dean played a significant role across our club’s first decade in the competition, and his expertise and industry experience will be instrumental in helping us take steps forward in the years ahead,” Gold Coast’s general manager of football Craig Cameron said.

Solomon said the Suns job aligned with his family circumstances .

“The opportunity to return to the Gold Coast Suns to work alongside and learn from Damien Hardwick and an experienced group of coaches is one I’m really excited by,” Solomon said.

“The potential of the list that has been assembled is incredibly inviting and I see it as an exciting time to be part of the Suns.

“The Gold Coast and Northern New South Wales has been home for my family and I for over 16 years now, so to be able to be with my wife and kids again and still coach at the highest level at a club where I’ve previously spent 10 years, is something I’m very grateful for.”

#5457. Une grand-mère avec des lunettes de soleil devient une icône insolite de la mode

Une grand-mère de la Zambie rurale est devenue une icône de style et une sensation sur Internet - après avoir accepté de jouer à s'habiller et à échanger des tenues avec sa petite-fille fashionista.

Margret Chola, qui a plus de 80 ans, est connue dans le monde entier sous le nom de "Légendaire Glamma" - et adorée par 225 000 adeptes d'Instagram pour ses photographies de mode saisissantes et ludiques.

"Je me sens différente, je me sens nouvelle et vivante dans ces vêtements, d'une manière que je n'ai jamais ressentie auparavant", déclare Mme Chola à la BBC. "J'ai l'impression de pouvoir conquérir le monde !"

La série bimensuelle Granny Series a été créée en 2023 par sa petite-fille Diana Kaumba, une styliste basée à New York.

L'idée lui est venue lors d'une visite en Zambie à l'occasion du deuxième anniversaire de la mort de son père, qui, selon elle, a inspiré sa passion pour la mode parce qu'il s'habillait toujours bien.

Lors de cette visite, Mme Kaumba n'avait pas porté toutes les tenues qu'elle avait soigneusement sélectionnées. Elle a donc demandé à sa grand-mère - ou « Mbuya » en langue bemba - si elle voulait les essayer.

"Je ne faisais rien à ce moment-là, alors j'ai dit : "OK, si c'est ce que tu veux faire, faisons-le, pourquoi pas ?" Mme Chola a ajouté : "Je vous manquerai quand je mourrai."

"Je vous manquerai quand je mourrai et au moins, de cette façon, vous vous souviendrez de moi."

Mme Kaumba portait le haut de Mbuya et un "chitenge" - un morceau de tissu à motifs enroulé autour de la taille. La première tenue de Mbuya était un tailleur pantalon argenté.

"J'ai pensé qu'il serait agréable d'habiller Mbuya à la mode et de la photographier ensuite dans son habitat naturel", explique Mme Kaumba à la BBC.

Cet habitat naturel est une ferme située dans le village de 10 Miles, juste au nord de la capitale zambienne, Lusaka.

Le plus souvent, Mme Chola est photographiée dans toute sa splendeur à l'extérieur, souvent assise sur une élégante chaise en bois ou allongée sur un canapé en cuir.

À l'arrière-plan, on aperçoit des bâtiments en briques apparentes avec des toits en tôle ondulée, des champs labourés, des manguiers et des cultures de maïs.

"J'étais tellement nerveuse lorsque j'ai posté cette première photo. J'ai laissé mon téléphone pendant 10 minutes et, dans ces 10 minutes, il y a eu 1 000 likes", raconte Mme Kaumba.

"J'en ai eu le souffle coupé. Les commentaires fusaient et les gens en redemandaient".

C'est en avril 2024 que les "Granny Series" ont vraiment décollé, après que Mme Kaumba a posté une série de photos de sa grand-mère vêtue d'une robe Adidas rouge, de plusieurs gros colliers dorés et d'une couronne de bijoux étincelante.

"J'ai été surprise d'apprendre que tant de gens m'aimaient dans le monde entier", déclare Mme Chola, qui ne connaît pas son âge exact car elle n'a pas d'acte de naissance.

"Je ne savais pas que je pouvais avoir un tel impact à cet âge."

Mme Chola pose dans des vêtements qui sont un mélange de couleurs vives, de textures et de styles.

Un maillot de football américain vert, associé à une robe rouge à froufrous superposée et stylisée comme une jupe - aux couleurs du drapeau zambien pour rendre hommage aux 60 ans d'indépendance.

Un haut à paillettes bleu, noir et vert, accompagné d'un collier et d'un bracelet en serpent doré.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

Et la préférée de Mbuya : un jean, un T-shirt graphique à son effigie et une perruque blonde.

"Je n'avais jamais porté de jeans ni de perruque auparavant, alors j'étais heureuse et je dansais".

Mme Kaumba, qui est styliste depuis 2012, affirme que sa grand-mère a "du courage, de la grâce et qu'elle réussit tous les looks".

Tous les looks reflètent son esthétique maximaliste-chic, qui célèbre la joie de l'excès, les combinaisons éclectiques, le grand et l'audacieux, ainsi que les motifs et les couleurs qui s'entrechoquent.

Au cœur de tout cela se trouvent des accessoires qui attirent le regard : lunettes de soleil audacieuses, chapeaux surdimensionnés, colliers, bracelets, pendentifs, bagues, gants, sacs, perruques blondes, couronnes.

Cette influence lui vient directement de sa grand-mère, qui a "toujours aimé les perles et les bracelets".

Dans une scène particulièrement ludique intitulée GOAT - abréviation de greatest of all time (le plus grand de tous les temps) - Mme Chola apparaît avec une chèvre - qui est parée des perles chères à Mbuya.

D'autres accessoires reflètent également la personnalité et l'histoire de Chola.

Sur certaines photos, Mbuya tient sa radio bien-aimée qu'elle transporte toute la journée et qu'elle emporte avec elle au lit.

Elle tient aussi un "ibende", un long bâton de bois qu'elle a utilisé au fil des ans pour piler le millet, le manioc ou le maïs.

Elle fume une pipe ou tient une tasse en métal remplie de thé, et pend au bord du bras de la chaise un "mbaula" ou brasero à charbon de bois que les Zambiens utilisent souvent pour cuisiner - surtout depuis que le pays est en proie à de graves coupures d'électricité.

Mme Kaumba espère que la série « Granny Series » mettra en évidence le fait que les personnes âgées ont encore beaucoup à offrir - et que créer des souvenirs ensemble est un moyen important de "laisser des traces pour la prochaine génération".

"Ne les rayez pas de la carte, aimez-les jusqu'à la fin, car n'oubliez pas que nous serons comme eux un jour".

Suite aux séances de photos de Mbuya, Mme Kaumba a été engagée par quatre petites-filles pour coiffer leurs grands-mères, âgées de 70 à 96 ans.

Mme Chola espère que la série « Granny » incitera les gens à « vivre leur vie sans se soucier d'être jugés par la société ».

Elle invite les gens à "toujours se pardonner les erreurs qu'ils ont commises. On ne peut jamais changer son passé, mais on peut changer son avenir".

Les séances photo ont rapproché la petite-fille et la grand-mère, et grâce à ce lien spécial, Mme Kaumba en a appris beaucoup plus sur la vie souvent difficile de sa Mbuya.

Mme Chola a été élevée par ses grands-parents, est allée à l'école jusqu'à l'âge de 12 ou 13 ans, puis, pour des raisons économiques, a été forcée d'épouser un homme d'une trentaine d'années.

Elle a eu trois enfants, s'est mise à boire beaucoup et a fini par échapper au mariage.

Ce traumatisme la hante encore, mais sa célébrité mondiale inattendue lui a redonné goût à la vie.

"Je peux maintenant me réveiller avec un but en sachant que les gens du monde entier aiment me voir", dit Chola.

Penny Dale est une journaliste indépendante, podcasteur et documentariste basée à Londres.

#5460. Sunday storm lashes Canberra, leaving trail of blackouts and fallen trees

A fierce Sunday afternoon storm has lashed Canberra, felling trees, snapping power lines and leaving many households across the territory without electricity.

The ACT Emergency Services Agency (ESA) confirmed no injuries were reported, despite a tree crushing a parked car in Griffith and another smashing into the roof of a house in Giralang.

Crews received 27 calls for assistance on Sunday afternoon after damaging winds and heavy rain battered the capital.

Tree damage was widespread across both north and south Canberra, with suburbs including Red Hill, Wanniassa, Kambah and parts of Belconnen bearing the brunt.

ACT State Emergency Service (SES) volunteers were deployed across the city to clear roads and properties. By 5pm, crews had attended to more than 10 jobs, with teams working well into the evening to clear debris.

In Giralang, SES personnel were called to Leneham Street about 5.30pm to cut away a large branch that had crashed through the roof of a house.

Fallen power lines caused widespread outages across Turner, Hughes, Kambah, Evatt and Narrabundah. While some residents experienced only brief interruptions, others were left without power for several hours as line crews worked to restore the network.

#5461. Singapore leaders condemn deadly church attack in Jordan, convey condolences to victims' families

Gunmen killed at least nine people and injured about 40 others on Friday when they opened fire during a funeral procession at St George’s Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan.

Cleaners and others gather outside St George's Greek Orthodox Church a day after gunmen opened fire during a funeral in the village of Hamoud, in Jordan's Karak governorate, on Oct 24, 2026. (Photo: AP/Raad Adayleh)

SINGAPORE: President Tharman Shanmugaratnam and Prime Minister Lawrence Wong have expressed their condolences over a deadly attack at a church in Jordan, condemning the deliberate targeting of civilians at a place of worship.

Gunmen killed at least nine people and injured about 40 others on Friday (Oct 23) when they opened fire during a funeral procession at the church in the village of Hammoud in southern Jordan's Karak governorate.

The assailants fled after the shooting, prompting a manhunt by security forces.

In a letter to Jordan's King Abdullah II, dated Oct 26, President Tharman said he was "deeply shocked by the horrific attack" on St George's Greek Orthodox Church.

The deliberate targeting of civilians at a place of worship is reprehensible."Mr Tharman said Singapore stands in solidarity with Jordan and its people in the fight against terrorism "in any form and from any source"."I am confident that the people of Jordan will remain united in the face of this tragedy," he added.

"On behalf of the people of Singapore, I extend my heartfelt condolences and sympathies to Your Majesty and the families of the victims," he wrote.

"Singapore strongly condemns this senseless act of violence. The deliberate targeting of civilians at a place of worship is reprehensible."

Mr Tharman said Singapore stands in solidarity with Jordan and its people in the fight against terrorism "in any form and from any source".

"I am confident that the people of Jordan will remain united in the face of this tragedy," he added.

In a separate letter to his Jordanian counterpart Jafar Hassan, Mr Wong described the attack as an act of terrorism.

"Singapore strongly condemns the deliberate targeting of civilians at a place of worship," he wrote. "Such acts of violence are unconscionable and cannot be justified under any circumstances."

Mr Wong also extended his deepest condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a swift recovery.

"We stand firmly with Jordan in opposing terrorism and religious extremism, and in upholding the values of religious tolerance and peaceful coexistence," he added.

Jordan's King Abdullah II vowed a forceful response, saying the attack would be met with the "harshest retaliation".

Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also declared three days of national mourning, with flags flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.

Attacks on places of worship are rare in the Muslim-majority kingdom, where Christians account for about 2 to 3 per cent of the population.

#5463. Push for early train times to get FIFO workers to Perth Airport

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Perth Airport boss Jason Waters is “confident” the state government will tinker with its train timetable to better cater the Airport Line for fly-in, fly-out workers.

FIFO workers considering public transport for their flight days have long complained the Airport Line service does not run early enough to catch the morning peak of FIFO flights, which runs from about 4am to 8am.

The earliest train to the Airport Central station arrives at 5.27am, but for most intrastate flights, check in closes 30 minutes before the flight time – making it nearly impossible to catch a 6am flight using the train.

Asked about a FIFO service at a press conference on Monday, Waters said he was in constant communication with the government in relation to both road and rail.

“I’m certain that as the airport grows and the needs of passengers become more clear and understood, I’m confident that we’ll see the availability of train follow suit,” he said.

In the past, the WA government has been reluctant to extend train operating hours, because it would shorten maintenance windows on the city’s rail network.

At the same press conference on Monday, Premier Roger Cook said Transport Minister Rita Saffioti was always reviewing timetables to make sure they served the community

“That’s why you’ve seen millions of people shifting onto rail, taking part in the expansion of Metronet as paying passengers,” he said.

According to the latest Public Transport Authority annual report, boardings on the Airport line increased 11 per cent from 2024-25 to 2025-26, rising from 5.62 million boardings to 6.23 million.

Perth Airport will want to see as many people as possible coming to the airport on public transport as it gears up for one of the biggest transformations in the airport’s history.

Construction will begin in the coming months on $5 billion worth of work, including a third runway and new terminal which will bring Qantas’ extensive Perth operations under the same roof as all other carriers at Terminal 1.

At the same time, another carpark and a new hotel will be built near Terminal 1, prompting a warning from Waters that “the journey ahead is going to be tricky.”

“We’re going to be bringing thousands of construction workers onto the terminal site, and that means there are going to be delays and challenges for passengers but we’re going to remain open 24/7 through the entire construction period,” he said.

“Don’t get caught out last minute because from here on in, over the next five or six years, there’s going to be a lot happening at Perth Airport.”

Waters revealed only 4 per cent of passengers to Perth Airport used the train to come or go from the airport, driven in part because there was no train servicing the Qantas terminals.

However, he said once the airport was all under one roof the Airport Line would be a much more attractive option.

“The construction of the one airport model gives us the ability to really go to the people of Perth and Western Australia with a proposition that says use the train because we’re all in one place now,” he said.

Speaking on the 40th anniversary of the opening of Terminal 1, Waters said the airport upgrades were expected to be completed by 2031 and the timing and cost was still on target, but work was still being done on the final time and cost.

Perth Airport will be competing with mining, defence and the state government for materials and labour.

More than $25 billion worth of work is under way at Henderson to prepare for AUKUS, billions are being spent on grid upgrades, and renewable energy projects and tens of thousands of homes are being built.

Waters wasn’t worried about the competition in the state’s already hot construction sector.

“I think it’s actually exciting times for Western Australia. The AUKUS investment, the ongoing investment the state government’s making, as well as Perth Airport, it’s all part of what makes the package of Western Australia great,” he said.

“What is important is that in the background we are having conversations to ensure that we schedule things in a way that enable it all to be achieved in a sensible manner. So I’m not asking that anything be slowed down.”

Cook said the Office of Major Infrastructure Delivery was working with big constructors to work out timings of project to avoid labor and materials constraints.

“There’s timing around concrete, timing around rebar and other steel products to make sure that they can all work in concert with each other,” he said.

#5464. The Pitt made her a breakout star overnight. She thinks that's the problem

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.

Shabana Azeez thinks fame is bad for your health.

But since landing the role of medical student Victoria Javadi on HBO Max's The Pitt — a show that swept last year's awards season, taking home five Emmys and two Golden Globes — the 29-year-old Adelaidian has had a front-row seat to what being a rising star actually does to a person.

For Azeez, the experience has brought an expected lesson about success: even as her career takes off in Hollywood, home — and the ordinariness that comes with it — remains her way of keeping perspective.

"I think fame is bad for your health," Azeez tells SBS News.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

"It's not that I'm famous or anything — thank God — but there is that kind of thing starting and happening in these small ways. It's bad for you."

"I think it's really good for your soul to get off the chessboard a little bit," she says.

It's a grounded way to talk about a career that, by any measure, is having a moment.

The Pitt turned Azeez into one of the more closely watched Australian acting newcomers in recent years — a stardom made stranger by the fact that she remained largely incognito at home even as the show became an international hit.

The series has since been renewed for a third season, giving Azeez another opportunity to build on the role that brought her to a global audience.

When she flew to Los Angeles to shoot the medical drama, she wasn't chasing a long-held plan, and she certainly wasn't arriving fresh out of drama school — she'd actually been rejected from one years earlier.

She got there through a mix of good luck and bad: a safer arts admin job after drama school rejection, then a boss who, sensing her heart wasn't in the work, booked her an audition for a short film without asking (thankfully, she landed it).

That opportunity pulled her into Adelaide's indie filmmaking scene, eventually leading to her feature debut in 2023's Birdeater and, after the film screened internationally, to US representation and an audition for The Pitt.

Growing up in Adelaide, the daughter of Indo-Fijian migrants, Azeez never really considered acting an option.

"The narrative was: do not become an actor, so help me, God," she says of her parents' position.

"It's not unreasonable for migrant parents — who've given up their culture and their home to give you financial stability, security and safety — it's not unreasonable for them to say, 'I gave up everything to give you safety. Please don't mess this up.'"

Even now, as her profile continues to rise, Azeez talks about the industry as if she's still waiting for her luck to run out.

"It works out for very few actors. This is not a job people can do full-time for a wage — you hit the jackpot or you don't," she says. "It might all go away tomorrow — there's no guarantee."

That first year in Los Angeles filming The Pitt was, on paper, her dream coming true. In practice, it felt more like grief.

"I spent the first year I was here just being devastated and feeling the injustice that my family's not from here, that other people can live out their dreams of being an actor and don't have to leave everything they know behind," she says.

What eventually helped her find her footing was keeping one foot firmly in the life she's left behind. Each Christmas, she flies back to Adelaide, where her newfound success is treated less like an achievement and more like material for a stand-up comedy show.

"If somebody asked me a question at Christmas, before I could answer, my uncle would go, 'Action!'," she says.

"Now, I'm so grateful for the deeply aggressively normal circumstances of my childhood. I feel very grounded when I go home to Adelaide."

Azeez's next project brought her back to Australian soil for a different reason.

In The Airport Chaplain, Azeez plays Mira Ansari-Cole — the new airport manager of a bustling international terminal, clashing with veteran fixer Tobias Wallace (Hugo Weaving), whom she sees more as a liability than a saviour.

The eight-part SBS Original drama, filmed in Melbourne, premieres on SBS and SBS On Demand on 26 August before streaming globally on Netflix outside Australia.

It's Azeez's first major role back home since her international breakout.

She doesn't have children and jokes that she can't even keep plants alive, but playing a working mother in a leadership role still pulled her close to home.

"Growing up, my mum loved her job and left her job to take care of us because she didn't have enough help to be able to work and take care of the kids," she says.

She sees little that's changed since, pointing to how much harder and more expensive it's become to raise children while working: "It's really abysmal that it's no better for women now."

In every role she takes on, Azeez talks about impact: Lesbian Space Princess was a vehicle for queer joy, The Pitt was a show centred on the pressures facing healthcare workers. The Airport Chaplain, she says, is for working mums.

"My career has been about representing young women as messy and still worthy of empathy. Now as I get older, that's where I want my career to go."

That framing shapes how she relates to Mira.

"I think it's really important that women don't have to be nice to be likeable or even just to be respected — you shouldn't have to be nice or gentle or accommodating," she says. "For me, that was Mira's quiet power — not pandering to the old way of doing things."

It's a lesson she's trying to take into her own life.

"I want everybody to be happy and I want to be easy to work with … but it's impossible to go into work with 200 people every day and to have all of them be pleased with you in every single moment."

"That's hypervigilance that I think I need to get rid of."

Azeez is acutely aware of what her presence on screen can mean to other people, particularly Australian women of colour who rarely see themselves centred in Australian television and film.

"It's such an honour to make people's lives better, to make people less alone, to make people feel like they can dream," she says.

"It's really hard to be mentorless and not see any pathways forward for where you want to go — so in any way that I can help people feel like they're not living on the tightrope between two cultures, that they're actually living on a superhighway with a bunch of other people on it — that's an honour."

But she resists being cast as a trailblazer.

"It just means that if you are the person who finally gets a seat at the table, it means you're sitting at the table with a bunch of people who don't understand where you came from."

Her reluctance to embrace the label reflects the tension of being called a 'first', when that recognition can also carry the weight of what it took to get there.

"[If people say] I'm the first Fijian-Indian person to do something, I think that it's actually not impressive. It's heartbreaking for everybody who came before me.

"I'm happy for the impact I'm having on anybody who's going to come after me, but it's not a thing of pride. I'm proud — but I'm not proud."

All eight episodes of The Airport Chaplain will be available to stream on SBS On Demand from Wednesday 26 August. The first two episodes premiere on SBS at 8.30pm on 26 August, with double episodes continuing to air weekly on Wednesdays at 8.30pm.

#5465. Shooters wary of surrendering firearms as confusion surrounds NSW gun buyback

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Doubts are mounting over how many people will participate in the first stage of NSW’s controversial gun buyback scheme as confusion lingers over which shooters qualify for exemptions to the caps.

The first buyback appointments opened on Monday ahead of the November 2 start date for the scheme, but farming and shooting groups have questioned how many will willingly take part without knowing if they qualify for an exemption next year.

The government introduced a four-gun cap for most shooters, with farmers and sporting shooters granted a 10-gun cap, under legislation rushed through the parliament in the wake of the Bondi terror attack in which 15 people were killed and dozens of others injured.

Under a draft regulation, a further exemption to the cap would be considered by the police commissioner on a case-by-case basis if gun owners have a genuine need for each additional firearm above the cap.

A NSW government statement said police will conduct “targeted consultation” on the regulation.

Police Minister Yasmin Catley said circumstances that may qualify for an exemption include farmers with guns at multiple properties, or elite sporting shooters who need different guns for different sporting events.

“We’re just making sure people have all the right information, so they can make a decision about how they want to deal with the guns that they have and how they choose to participate in the buyback,” Catley said.

Bookings opened at noon on Monday for gun owners to surrender their guns at six police stations: Narellan, Penrith, Sutherland, Griffith, Grafton and Dubbo. A further 34 stations will participate in the scheme in the coming months.

The first stage of the scheme will offer compensation of up to $1000 for each gun. Compensation for higher value firearms will come next year.

By 5pm on Monday 100 gun owners had registered to take part in the buyback, and 30 had made appointments for the first week.

NSW Farmers Association rural affairs committee vice chair Glen Andreazza said he would be surprised if any farmers participated in the buyback before knowing what the regulations for exemptions included.

“There would be no reason for a farmer to surrender any weapons at this point in time,” he said.

Sporting Shooters Association Australia is encouraging members to comply with the law. However, NSW chief executive Pete Szaak said the uncertainty around who would qualify for an exemption made it unlikely sporting shooters would voluntarily surrender guns in the first stage of the buyback.

Szaak said the looming regulations raised more questions than answers, leaving some sporting shooters confused.

“Given there is no requirement to compulsorily hand guns in, you should think about all these things first … it’s not as if police are ripping doors down doing search warrants,” he said.

While the state Labor government has committed to taking the gun crackdown to the election, the Shooters Union is encouraging members to boycott the buyback. The Coalition and One Nation have called for the firearms caps to be repealed.

Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane, who voted with the government to support the gun crackdown after the Bondi attack, has said the Liberals would scrap caps for farmers and sporting shooters.

A recent Resolve Political Monitor survey found voters were overwhelmingly in favour of caps on the number of firearms an individual can own and time limits on gun licences.

In the survey of voters in August and September, 80 per cent said they supported restricting gun licences to Australian citizens, 73 per cent favoured the four-gun cap for individuals, and 75 per cent supported time limits on licences forcing owners to reapply every few years.

A majority – 53 per cent – said they supported the government’s buyback, which has drawn criticism from gun owners, the Coalition and some independent MPs. Only 20 per cent opposed the scheme, with 27 per cent either neutral or undecided.

#5467. Du surfeur olympique à Donald Trump : 12 des images les plus frappantes de 2024

De la photo impressionnante d'un surfeur à Tahiti à celle emblématique du président élu américain, Donald Trump, prise après une tentative d'assassinat, voici 12 des images les plus accrocheuses de l'année dernière.

Un avion traverse une éclipse solaire totale au-dessus de Bloomington, dans l'Indiana, le 8 avril – ses traînées prolongées se détachant contre une couronne scintillante.

Ce n'est bien sûr pas la première fois que les trajectoires d'un avion, de la lune, du soleil et de la Terre se croisent.

En janvier 1925, un dirigeable de la marine américaine, l'USS Los Angeles, était chargé de 500 livres (227 kg) de télescopes et des esprits de sept scientifiques pour observer de près une éclipse solaire très attendue dont le chemin passait directement au-dessus de New York, en faisant, selon certains, l'éclipse la plus observée de l'histoire.

Pas à bord, mais observant attentivement depuis son chevalet sur Terre, se trouvait le peintre américain Howard Russell Butler, qui a capturé l'événement comme le troisième panneau d'un triptyque d'éclipses époustouflantes (1918, 1923 et 1925) qu'il espérait inspirer les écoliers.

Connaître l'histoire de l'art peut vous éviter un stress et des chagrins considérables.

C'était, du moins, l'une des leçons tirées de la controverse entourant une photo d'un tableau décadent prise lors de la cérémonie d'ouverture des Jeux olympiques.

L'image, qui présente une table mise en scène de manière exagérée avec une figure nue allongée de manière décadente sur un plateau, entourée de drag queens et d'une chanteuse séduisante assise dans une coupe de fruits, a été prise pour une satire de La Cène par certains critiques chrétiens et conservateurs, qui ont condamné l'œuvre, la jugeant indécente, voire sacrilège.

S'excusant pour la confusion, le comité d'organisation de Paris 2024 a précisé que le tableau n'était pas du tout destiné à rappeler le chef-d'œuvre de Léonard de Vinci, mais à invoquer plutôt le dieu grec Dionysos, évoquant les contours d'une peinture ultérieure de Jan van Bijlert, Le Festin des dieux (1635).

Les réfugiés soudanais attendent leur tour pour recevoir de l'aide dans une file d'attente bondée au centre de transit de Renk, au Soudan du Sud, en février.

Au début de l'année, plus d'un demi-million de personnes ont fui les combats entre l'armée soudanaise et les Forces de soutien rapide paramilitaires... La fluidité joyeuse des tissus colorés et le rythme des motifs riches contrastent fortement avec la sobriété de la situation des migrants.

L'intensité de la photo rappelle le rythme et la texture des œuvres abstraites du célèbre artiste et cinéaste soudanais Hussein Shariffe, dont les peintures poétiques brouillaient la frontière entre les couleurs que nous voyons et celles que nous ressentons.

Crédit photo, AFP Photo/ Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation

Les images du puissant volcan indonésien Mont Ruang, qui a érupté plusieurs fois en avril, projetant de la lave chaude et des colonnes de cendres fumantes dans le ciel, étaient aussi fascinantes qu'elles étaient menaçantes.

La force redoutable de l'activité volcanique a fasciné les créateurs d'images pendant des millénaires et une photo de l'éruption sublime de téphra incandescent, de ponce vaporisée et de minerai fondu dans l'atmosphère était étrangement en accord avec la vision violente de l'artiste romantique britannique John Martin.

Il y a deux siècles, il a réimaginé l'éruption du Vésuve en 79 après J.-C. pour sa peinture apocalyptique La Destruction de Pompéi et d'Herculanum (1822).

Certaines photos se chorégraphient d'elles-mêmes, conscientes de leur propre iconicité durable.

Le lever du drapeau américain sur Iwo Jima, par exemple, ou le lever de poings en signe de Black Power par des athlètes américains lors de la cérémonie de remise des médailles aux Jeux olympiques d'été de 1968 à Mexico, viennent à l'esprit.

Évoquant des éléments des deux jalons de la création d'image, la photo d'un Donald Trump défiant, levant le poing, se relevant avec le visage couvert de sang après qu'un prétendu assassin lui a percé l'oreille droite d'une balle, lors d'un rassemblement électoral en juillet, tandis qu'un Stars and Stripes déséquilibré se penche derrière lui, a fait se demander à beaucoup si c'était le moment où il a gagné l'élection.

Deux filles palestiniennes, se préparant pour le ramadan, allument des lanternes pour décorer des tentes de réfugiés bondées dans le sud de Gaza, le 29 février.

La douce lumière des lanternes contraste fortement avec la lueur étrange d'un coucher de soleil incertain scintillant au loin. De cette période à l'été, 90 % des Gazaouis (environ deux millions de personnes) auront été déplacés par la guerre.

L'acte enchanteur d'allumer des lanternes fait écho à une scène célèbre de l'histoire de l'art – le charmant portrait des filles de son ami par John Singer Sargent dans un jardin crépusculaire du sud-ouest de l'Angleterre, Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose, peint patiemment sur une période de plusieurs mois lorsque la lumière était juste parfaite pendant quelques instants fugaces, chaque soir à l'automne 1885.

Tout ce qui manque, c'est l'herbe verte et les fleurs sauvages, et un sentiment de paix durable.

L'image inspirante de Gabriel Medina du Brésil s'élevant vers le ciel après avoir affronté une énorme vague au large de l'île polynésienne de Tahiti, lors du troisième tour des séries de surf masculin, le 29 juillet, est instantanément devenue virale.

La lévitation apparemment sans effort de Medina rappelle d'innombrables représentations religieuses de l'ascension mystique dans l'art occidental, de Giotto à Rembrandt, d'Il Garofalo à Salvador Dalí.

Ce qui scelle la surprenante synchronicité de l'élévation athlétique avec l'ascension spirituelle, c'est le bras droit levé de Medina et la poussée froide de son index, pointant précisément vers l'endroit où son corps et son âme semblent se diriger.

Une habitante de Valence, en Espagne, regarde depuis son balcon, le 30 octobre, le quartier inondé en contrebas, tandis que des véhicules emportés se percutent, comme une ruée de taureaux de fer déferlant dans les rues.

Un phénomène météorologique connu sous le nom de DANA (Depresión Aislada de Niveles Altos), ou "goutte froide", a frappé Valence un jour plus tôt, déclenchant des pluies sans précédent.

En seulement huit heures, 500 mm (20 pouces) sont tombés, dévastant la région.

Le point de vue vertigineux de la femme valencienne, à travers les yeux de laquelle nous voyons le monde se plier et se tordre, rappelle la perspective froissée du tableau de 1912 du cubiste italien Carlo Carra, Simultaneità, La donna al balcone.

Lors d'une soirée d'écoute pour la sortie de son album Hit Me Hard and Soft à New York en mai, la chanteuse américaine Billie Eilish semble se dissoudre dans un rêve de lumière embrumée alors que son corps est à la fois amplifié et vaporisé en une silhouette imposante, bien que intangible.

La dissolution de soi dans une brume resplendissante rappelle les visions évaporées du peintre britannique JMW Turner, dont la peinture complexe Light and Colour (Goethe's Theory) - the Morning after the Deluge (1843), imagine un moment apparemment insondable d'illumination sublime, qui prépare la scène pour chaque nuance scintillante de l'existence qui suit.

Dans un geste de mépris profond, un groupe de personnes piétine la tête d'une statue renversée de l'ancien président Hafez al-Assad, le 9 décembre, en Syrie.

Après l'effondrement du régime Baas de la Syrie et la fuite de la famille Assad du pays, les Syriens ont été vus en train de détruire d'innombrables effigies du père du président destitué Bachar al-Assad dans les villes du pays.

Il y a, bien sûr, une sorte de catharsis collective dans la jubilation partagée de détruire les statues des dirigeants rejetés, comme nous le voyons dans la peinture de William Walcutt de 1857 représentant un cercle de New-Yorkais en extase abattant la statue du roi George III par le sculpteur britannique Joseph Wilton en juillet 1776, à la suite d'une lecture enflammée de la Déclaration d'indépendance fraîchement adoptée.

En avril, plus de 350 danseurs se sont réunis pour établir le record du monde Guinness du plus grand nombre de ballerines posant simultanément en pointe.

Une photo de nombreux participants se préparant avec excitation pour la compétition a capturé l'élégance et l'énergie de cet événement mémorable.

La foule claustrophobe de tant de jeunes femmes aurait sans doute plu à l'artiste impressionniste français Edgar Degas, qui, semble-t-il, ne se contentait pas d'apprécier la vue des danseuses habiles, qu'il appelait ses "petites guenons", en train de s'entraîner et de se produire, mais aussi le son angoissant de leurs articulations "craquant". "J'en ai peut-être trop souvent", avoua-t-il au peintre Pierre-Georges Jeanniot, "considéré la femme comme un animal".

Une Sud-Coréenne saisit sans peur le canon du fusil chargé d'un soldat.

Capturée peu après que le président Yoon Suk Yeol a déclaré la loi martiale, l'image montre Ahn Gwi-ryeong, 35 ans, porte-parole du parti d'opposition démocrate, luttant avec des soldats lourdement armés, qui avaient reçu l'ordre d'empêcher les députés de se rassembler.

"Ma seule pensée, a déclaré plus tard Ahn à propos de la confrontation, était que je devais simplement les arrêter. Je les ai repoussés, les ai secoués, et j'ai fait tout ce que j'ai pu."

La détermination inflexible d'Ahn et même le scintillement de la lumière métallique sur ses vêtements rappellent le portrait aquarelle émouvant de Jeanne d'Arc par l'artiste britannique John Gilbert au 19e siècle.

#5469. Vier Fragen an Sandra Wollner zu "Everytime"

Die österreichische Regisseurin geht mit ihrem rätselhaften Trauerdrama für Deutschland ins Oscar-Rennen. Auf der Viennale feiert "Everytime" Österreichpremiere

Birgit Minichmayrs Ella reist mit ihrer jungen Tochter Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling) und Lux (Tristán López), dem Ex-Freund ihrer Älteren, nach Teneriffa, wo ebenso rätselhafte wie heilsame Dinge passieren.

Sandra Wollner, die aus Leoben stammende, 43-jährige Regisseurin, kann auf ein echtes Erfolgsjahr zurückblicken. Eine Selektion in Cannes im Wettbewerb Un Certain Regard, der Hauptpreis dort, ebenso wie am Filmfestival von Sarajevo und eine Nominierung, um für Deutschland, wo sie lebt und arbeitet, ins Oscar-Rennen zu gehen. Grund dafür ist ihr komplexes, rätselhaftes Drama Everytime, in dem Birgit Minichmayr als alleinerziehende Mutter einen Trauerprozess zwischen Berlin und Teneriffa durchlebt. Wollner, die ihren Durchbruch 2020 im damals neu geschaffenen Berlinale-Wettbewerb Encounters mit ihrem zweiten Spielfilm The Trouble With Being Born hatte – ein die Gemüter spaltendes Drama rund um einen humanoiden Kinder- und Sexroboter – legt Everytime gegen jede Konvention an. Sie spart unmittelbare Trauerdarstellungen aus und flicht in ihre Erzählung ultrarealistische wie fantastische Elemente ein. Die Bilder suchen ungewöhnliche Perspektiven und Farben, lassen sich von Computerspielen ebenso inspirieren wie von schwindelerregenden, traumartigen Visionen. Irgendwann ist die gelb flirrende Sonne dann einfach viereckig und die Welt bleibt kurz stehen.

#5470. Thunderstorm asthma warning issued in the ACT following storm forecast

A thunderstorm asthma warning has been sounded for Canberra, with high levels of pollen and windy conditions forecast for Sunday.

In an official statement, the ACT government warned that high pollen levels, windy conditions and forecast storms have increased the risk of thunderstorm asthma on Sunday, October 25, across the ACT and surrounding region.

While anyone can be affected by thunderstorm asthma, those who have a history of, or currently suffer from asthma or hay fever are at higher risk of being affected.

In the event of a medical emergency, call Triple Zero (000) and stay indoors while waiting for an ambulance to arrive.

The Bureau of Meteorology forecast predicts a thunderstorm is likely on Sunday afternoon, possibly severe with damaging winds, large hail and heavy rain which may lead to flash flooding.

An increased risk means a thunderstorm asthma event is possible, but thunderstorm asthma events are rare, the ACT government said.

More information about the thunderstorm asthma alert can be found at Public health alert: Possible Thunderstorm Asthma Event for the ACT

#5472. Man dies after landslide hits two-storey house in Penang

Preliminary findings indicate that a leaking water pipe at a hillside construction project may have triggered the landslide, local authorities said.

An exposed hillside following a landslide in Paya Terubong, Penang, on Oct 26, 2026. (Photo: Facebook/Majlis Bandaraya Pulau Pinang - MBPP)

SINGAPORE: A man died after a landslide struck a house in Penang on Sunday (Oct 25), local authorities said.

The Penang Fire and Rescue Department said it responded to an emergency call at 8.36am after a landslide hit a two-storey house in the district of Taman Seri Rambai, Paya Terubong.

Three people were caught in the landslide, but while two were rescued, a 73-year-old man was trapped under the debris.

He was later pronounced dead at the scene by rescue workers, and his body was retrieved at about 11am.

The Penang Island City Council issued a stop-work order to a hillside condominium construction site located near the landslide, which council mayor A Rajendran later said was to facilitate authorities' investigations into the incident.

“The road and condominium projects have been ongoing for more than a year, while slope stabilisation works are also being carried out in the area,” he told the Bernama news agency.

However, Penang state executive councillor for Infrastructure, Transport and Digital Zairil Khir Johari said that stabilisation works had not yet been completed in some sections when the landslide occurred.

“Unfortunately, the section that had yet to be completed was the one affected by the landslide,” he told Bernama, adding that further investigations are ongoing.

Despite the dry weather, soil movement can still be detected at the landslide site, said northeast district officer Isma Suhaimi Shairff.

Preliminary findings indicate that a leaking water pipe on the slope and clogged drains may have caused water to accumulate, triggering the landslide, Bernama reported him as saying.

He added that a heavy crane and large concrete blocks at the site could fall if the ground shifts further.

Meanwhile, the exposed slope will be covered with plastic sheeting to protect it from rain, and six houses in the area have been ordered to evacuate, Isma Suhaimi said.

Updated - October 26, 2026 11:37 am IST - Beijing

Chinese President Xi Jinping. File | Photo Credit: AP

China’s President Xi Jinping opened a key meeting of Communist Party elites in Beijing on Monday (October 26, 2026), state media said, which observers will be closely watching for clues as to the country’s direction and future leadership.

Roughly 300 members of the ruling Communist Party’s Central Committee in attendance at the meeting, called the fifth plenum, will be looking to tighten discipline within their ranks, according to state media.

That includes measures to reduce corruption and make cadres more effective and loyal.

Mr. Xi opened the session on Monday (October 26, 2026), presenting a draft decision by the Central Committee that “sets out strategic plans for strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance”, state news agency Xinhua reported.

Few details from the closed-door gathering, held under tight security, will be made known until it concludes on Thursday (October 29, 2026), but the timing of the meeting is crucial.

The fifth plenum comes ahead of a major party congress next year, where 73-year-old Mr. Xi is almost certain to secure a historic fourth term and oversee a leadership reshuffle.

Previous plenums have represented key moments for Mr. Xi to cement his authority.

The Chinese leader has waged a 14-year campaign against corruption that has purged thousands of officials, including dozens of the Central Committee.

Yet he remains frustrated with cadres he deems are not implementing his orders.

State media published an article ahead of the plenum, based on a speech Mr. Xi gave in January in which he railed against “two-faced” officials who appear to comply with central directives but “inwardly resist”, pursue “individualism” and are “politically opportunistic”.

Analysts told AFP that Mr. Xi is trying to maximise efficiency and loyalty among cadres by imposing more supervision and rules.

But as a result of his expansive purges, this year’s plenum is expected to have the lowest turnout since former leader Mao Zedong’s death in 1976.

Eight of the Central Committee’s seats lie vacant, with another 15 members under investigation and at risk of being replaced.

Mr. Xi’s anti-corruption drive has also targeted the military, toppling five of the seven members of the Central Military Commission (CMC), the party’s top armed forces body.

Of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022, only two have not been purged or disappeared, according to the Asia Society Policy Institute.

The plenum could see new members appointed to the CMC; the party could wait until next year’s congress to replenish it; or Xi might even restructure party control over its vast military.

The talks also come at an unsteady time for the world’s second-largest economy, which has struggled to address persistently sluggish domestic spending and a protracted crisis in the crucial property sector.

Turbulent political and economic ties with the United States are also weighing on China’s leaders.

Authorities are expected to release a summary of the outcomes after the meeting concludes on Thursday (October 29, 2026).

#5474. Faster than Usain Bolt: The five-day robot Olympics putting humanoid autonomy to the test

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

Humanoid robots are racing, lifting, throwing and even playing tennis in Beijing this week, as China puts its rapidly advancing robotics industry through its paces.

The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games bring together more than 50 events, from traditional sports such as the 100m sprint and tug-of-war to challenges modelled on factory floors, restaurants, offices and emergency scenes.

But behind the spectacle and record-breaking times, the real competition is less about how fast a robot can run than how well it can cope when things go wrong.

Organisers are testing whether machines can see, think and respond to the messy unpredictability of the real world, and whether they can eventually perform useful work without a human stepping in.

The games, heavily promoted in Chinese state media, feature 51 events, including 30 sports competitions and 21 scenario-based contests.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

More than 40 per cent of the events require robots to operate fully autonomously, according to Huawei, a tech partner of the games.

The event is in its second year, and some robots are already outperforming the 2025 results.

On Saturday, two robots ran faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second world record in the 100m sprint. That was a sharp improvement from 2025, when the winning robot's time was more than 20 seconds.

Braking was an issue, as the machines slammed into a thick mat that organisers placed several metres after the finish line.

Another humanoid, the same model as the 100m champion, ran 400 metres in 39.7 seconds, faster than South African Wayde van Niekerk's world record of 43.03 seconds.

"The intensity is higher than last year, which places significant demands on the robot's battery management and thermal dissipation capabilities," said spectator and robotics investor Xu Qiaosheng.

"It holds huge significance for the development of China's industrial sector."

Robots will compete in tug-of-war and weightlifting, while Tai Chi and pitch-pot — in which contestants throw arrow-like sticks into a narrow-necked vase — will give traditional Chinese sports a futuristic twist.

Beyond the spectacle, the more revealing tests could come when robots encounter the small imperfections of the physical world: a cable at the wrong angle, an object just out of reach, a shifting package or a missed step.

That tests whether robots can identify objects, accurately position their hands and bodies, apply controlled force and recover from errors without human intervention.

Lumos Robotics Chief Executive Yu Chao said the games could help improve hardware and provide a showcase for the industry. But Yu said the longer-term value will depend on real-world problem solving.

"Only when it can work in those end scenarios does it have real value. Simply running and jumping does not improve efficiency," he added.

In addition to more familiar events drawn from human sports, robots will compete in EV charging, restaurant work, emergency incident handling and hand-dexterity contests.

There are also industrial assembly and material loading events. A cable connection challenge is a test of vision, mechanical alignment and force control.

Beijing-based robotics startup Galbot said it would stage an autonomous humanoid tennis match, with robots competing in singles and doubles, including ball tracking, serving, and returning shots.

For Hua Rong, chief marketing officer at robotics firm Zeroth, the real test will come after the demonstrations end.

"The competition will be whether, after the product is sold, it can really solve users' problems," she said.

#5478. Ce que révèle une vue à vol d'oiseau de l'Afrique

Au cours des 40 dernières années, Edward Burtynsky a photographié l'impact de l'industrie humaine sur la planète. Pour sa dernière collection, African Studies, il a parcouru le continent en prenant des photos d'en haut. Il s'est entretenu avec Mary Harper, de la BBC.

À bien des égards, c'est la Chine qui m'a donné envie de m'intéresser au continent africain.

Il y a une vingtaine d'années, j'ai photographié l'extraordinaire explosion de l'industrie manufacturière en Chine, usines comprises.

Des copies conformes de ces usines apparaissent aujourd'hui sur tout le continent et la ressemblance avec ce que j'ai vu il y a des décennies est troublante.

Alors que la Chine s'apprête à devenir une économie de services, elle délocalise ses méga-usines dans des pays comme l'Afrique du Sud, se lance dans d'immenses projets d'infrastructure et exploite les ressources du continent pour alimenter sa croissance.

La plupart de ces photos ont été prises du ciel, à partir d'avions, d'hélicoptères et de drones.

Elles révèlent la conception, la structure et l'échelle des marques que l'homme inscrit sur la terre, les panoramas extraordinaires qui ne sont pas visibles au niveau du sol.

À l'instar des industries extractives, l'agriculture suscite également des images abstraites lorsqu'elle est vue d'en haut.

Je me demande si les cueilleurs de thé et les cultivateurs de roses sont conscients de l'extraordinaire géométrie et symétrie des champs dans lesquels ils travaillent.

Ceux qui travaillent la terre, qu'elle soit fertile ou desséchée, en transforment parfois la beauté mais ne la détruisent pas.

En Afrique du Sud, les agriculteurs tentent de freiner la désertification en creusant de grandes ornières dans la terre qui recueillent l'eau lorsqu'il pleut, permettant ainsi aux plantes et aux arbres de pousser dans un environnement hostile.

Les terres africaines regorgent de ressources, certaines extraites à l'aide de technologies modernes, d'autres à l'aide de techniques vieilles de plusieurs siècles.

En Éthiopie, c'est comme si on remontait le temps en récoltant le sel à l'aide de pioches par des températures de 50 °C.

Chaque jour, le sel est chargé sur des chameaux, les bateaux du désert.

À Danakil, nous avons dû renoncer à nos instruments GPS. Comme la ville se trouve à environ 125 mètres au-dessous du niveau de la mer, les appareils se sont embrouillés, pensant que nous travaillions sous l'océan.

L'un des moments forts de mon voyage a été la visite des étangs salés du Sénégal, le plus grand producteur de sel d'Afrique de l'Ouest.

Les récolteurs creusent à la main des dépressions peu profondes qui sont ensuite remplies d'eau salée provenant des canaux voisins.

Une fois l'eau évaporée, les minéraux, les pigments et diverses algues se combinent aux reflets du ciel pour créer un spectacle pour l'œil. Les structures organiques complexes deviennent presque hypnotiques.

Le résultat brutal des profits des entreprises, de la pauvreté, de l'ingéniosité et de la piraterie impitoyable dans le delta du Niger, riche en pétrole, se classe facilement parmi les paysages les plus profondément troublants et dévastés jamais créés par l'humanité.

Le fait d'être confronté à l'expérience de ce paysage a constitué un tournant majeur dans ma compréhension du degré de souillure que nous sommes capables d'infliger à notre planète en tant qu'espèce.

Une différence frappante entre les usines chinoises et africaines est qu'en Afrique, l'essentiel de la main-d'œuvre provient des villes et des villages locaux, tandis que les chefs d'étage et les directeurs de site sont le plus souvent chinois.

Face à l'exode des populations vers les villes, la Chine s'est lancée dans une fièvre de construction qui empiète souvent sur de précieuses terres rurales.

Les montagnes Tsaus du Sperrgebiet, en Namibie, comptent parmi les formations terrestres les plus obsédantes et les plus belles que j'aie jamais photographiées.

Leurs structures topographiques et la richesse de leurs couleurs semblent transcender l'idée de paysage et entrer dans un domaine purement abstrait.

L'homo sapiens a commencé à migrer hors d'Afrique il y a environ 200 000 ans. Au XXIe siècle, la boucle est bouclée et nous retournons dans l'un des derniers endroits de la planète à avoir été balayé par les machinations implacables du complexe industriel humain.

Le continent africain est une frontière fragile et ultime.

Toutes les images sont soumises à des droits d'auteur.

#5479. Police searching for man who allegedly chased, threatened women near CBD fitness studio

Police are searching for a man who allegedly threatened and harassed multiple women on Northbourne Avenue in the city more than a week ago.

ACT Policing said about 5.30am on Thursday, October 15, police received reports of a man allegedly harassing multiple women near a fitness studio on Northbourne Avenue.

It is alleged the man chased several women, threatened to follow them into the fitness studio and attempted to kick one woman as she was walking towards the premises, police said.

The man allegedly returned the following morning and about 5.30am police once again received reports of a man matching the description engaging in similar behaviour at the same location.

Police allege the man again chased several women, threatened a female patron and threw a bottle in the direction of a woman as she fled.

Officers attended on both occasions and conducted extensive patrols of the surrounding area but were unable to locate the alleged offender, police said.

Following investigations, police are seeking the public's assistance to identify the man.

Police have released images of the man and have sought the public's assistance to locate him.

He is described as Caucasian in appearance, with a solid build and wavy hair.

He was wearing a grey cap, a red t-shirt over a cream-coloured long-sleeved shirt underneath, black board shorts, and white and brown shoes at the time of the incident, police said.

Anyone who can assist ACT Policing in the matter is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000, or via the Crime Stoppers ACT website quoting 8529138. Information can be provided anonymously.

Mariana Mazzucato legt auf Englisch eine „Gemeinwohl-Ökonomie“ vor, auf Deutsch ist daraus „Ein Kapitalismus, der allen nützt“ geworden

Will das Gemeinwohl ins Zentrum aller ökonomischen Beziehungen setzen: Die Ökonomin Mariana Mazzucato.

Ein Kapitalismus, der allen nützt, so der Titel des neuen Buches von Mariana Mazzucato, heißt im englischen Original The Common Good Economy. Sind mit der Übersetzung Kapitalismus und Gemeinwohl-Ökonomie auch schon gleichgesetzt? #5482. India's Infosys falls after revenue growth view cut flags AI, competitive pressures

FILE PHOTO: The Infosys logo is displayed during a press briefing, following the company's quarterly results announcement at its headquarters in Bengaluru, India, July 23, 2026. REUTERS/Priyanshu Singh/File Photo

Oct 26 : Shares of India's Infosys fell 2.7 per cent on Monday after the software exporter sharply cut its fiscal 2027 revenue growth forecast, underscoring challenges from AI-driven pricing pressure, tougher competition and sluggish demand in key markets.

The firm was the last of the top 5 to report earnings for the Indian IT sector. Earlier this month, peers Tata Consultancy Services and HCLTech met revenue estimates with modest margin performance, but investors cheered the uptick in AI revenue.

The company cut its fiscal 2027 revenue growth forecast to 1 per cent-2 per cent from 1.5 per cent-3 per cent, while most analysts had ​expected it to trim only the upper end of the range to 2.5 per cent.

"Peers are better placed than Infosys at this point, and the share movement is just reflecting that. Infosys has been underperforming from Q4FY26 results," LKP Securities analyst Anshul Jethi said.
