AI competition and clients expanding their global capability centres or offshore tech hubs directly, rather than engaging Infosys for IT services, are also hurting the company, he added.

Systematix analysts called it a "disappointing quarter", highlighting pricing pressure from heightened competition and client productivity demands on account of AI, and subdued tech spending among retail and high-tech clients.

Brokerage Motilal Oswal said weaker volumes, smaller-than-expected price increases, a shift toward offshore delivery and Infosys' decision to exit a large European manufacturing contract had weighed on growth.

Updated - October 26, 2026 11:48 am IST - SAO PAULO

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, greets supporters outside his residence on the day of the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil on October 25, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

In an election campaign that may be recorded in history for countering far-right tactics, defying foreign interference and social media manipulation, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a historic fourth presidential term, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro of Liberal Party (PL) in Brazil’s runoff elections on Sunday (October 25, 2026). Mr. Lula secured 64 million votes, the highest total ever recorded in a Brazilian presidential election, surpassing his own record of 60 million votes he received in 2022. Declaring a “defeat for lies and denialism”, he pledged to govern for all Brazilians and protect the country’s sovereignty. “Brazil is nobody’s backyard,” Mr. Lula declared at a midnight rally, sending a clear message to U.S. president Donald Trump as he addressed hundreds of thousands of supporters gathered along São Paulo’s iconic Avenida Paulista.

In an emotional speech, Mr. Lula thanked women and older voters for their support and praised the mobilisation of young people on the streets and on social media. “People went out to vote because we managed to convince them that their votes were extremely important to safeguarding democracy in the country,” he said. He also said he had learned many lessons from the election and promised to change his approach to governing, ensure greater public participation in government decisions and give digital communication a more prominent role during his fourth term. “The future begins today, and its name is youth. I salute the women who made all the difference. I salute the older people who made sacrifices and made their way to the polling stations to vote,” he said.

Mr. Lula secured an unprecedented comeback in the election. He trailed in the first round, receiving 45.16% of valid votes against 47.03% for Mr. Flávio. As the prospect of a Bolsonaro presidency caused a major concern among the young, especially about public education, healthcare and transport, millions of people joined weekly rallies across the country, pledging support for Mr. Lula and demanding protection of public services. On Sunday (October 25, 2026), Mr. Lula told his young supporters that their voices have been heard. “We will make increasing investment in in the Unified Health System, develop a national artificial intelligence system, continue to expand public universities and support the digital and creative economies,” Mr. Lula told his supporters with massive rounds of applause.

With most opinion polls predicting a neck-to-neck race and some even giving an edge to Mr. Flavio till a few days back, the Workers’ Party shifted its messaging from a comparison of the candidates’ personal records to a forward-looking agenda centred on concrete promises. Following the first-round results, Mr. Lula changed his campaign team’s leadership and began announcing measures such as an increase in direct cash transfer benefits, a new debt-relief programme, a package of benefits for small entrepreneurs and a pledge to make public transport free on weekends.

Even as Mr. Lula made these promises to the electorate, his campaign faced a big challenge: Big Tech firms – from Meta to X and Google – openly supported Mr. Flavio’s campaign while suppressing advertising by Mr. Lula’s team. In his speech on Sunday (October 25, 2026), Mr. Lula said he had to overcome “interference” by digital platforms and pledged to regulate big tech companies in Brazil. “This election was one in which we had to overcome interference coming from outside and through digital platforms. We will have to regulate them,” Mr. Lula said. On October 16 after an expose in the Brazilian media, Meta had admitted that its artificial intelligence tool had blocked the generation of campaign material supporting Mr. Lula while allowing the same technology to be used by the Flávio campaign.

With this historic mobilisation of people and a record victory, Mr. Lula also seems to have defeated Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly made clear that his preferred candidate in the race was Mr. Flávio. Now, Mr. Lula’s victory has applied brakes on the growing wave of right-wing leaders in the region. But Mr. Trump is not in a mood to throw in the towel. On Sunday (October 25, 2026) night, Mr. Trump questioned Mr. Lula’s victory, comparing it to the 2020 U.S. election which he lost to Joe Biden and alleged that Brazil had followed the “Joe Biden playbook.”

“Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite to win the second. But the communists never give up power once they get it,” Mr. Trump said, echoing the far-right’s strategy of questioning election results which do not go in their favour.

Mr. Flávio was singing the same tune on Sunday (October 25, 2026) night as he refused to accept the election result, announcing that he would seek the annulment of the election. He accused the Federal Supreme Federal of “changing the rules midway” after a judge ordered voting across the country to be extended until 7 p.m. when Mr. Lula complained about many right-wing mayors curtailing the bus services in the poor areas many cities. “It is impossible to recognise the election result in the context in which these things happened,” Mr. Flavio said, adding that his legal team would challenge the outcome.

It is a complete misreading of the mood in Brazil. After Mr. Lula finished his speech on Sunday (October 25, 2026) night, the crowd broke into a rendition of Brazil’s national independence song, sending a message to the far-right, Mr. Trump and Meta.

Supporters of Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, react to early result during the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil on October 25, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

#5486. L'artiste nigérian qui réinvente une vieillesse élégante par l'IA

Les œuvres d'art générées par l'intelligence artificielle (IA) sont devenues une source de controverse, mais le cinéaste et artiste nigérian Malik Afegbua défend l'idée qu'elle peut nous inciter à créer un monde réel meilleur - et un monde plus élégant pour les personnes âgées.

À première vue, ses images semblent avoir été prises sur le bord d'un podium de mode, mais ces modèles ne sont pas de vraies personnes.

Ces images sont le fruit de l'imagination d'Afegbua et d'un logiciel d'intelligence artificielle, et montrent des modèles d'un certain âge portant de beaux vêtements.

Il savait qu'il avait créé quelque chose de spécial après les avoir postées sur les médias sociaux. Surtout après qu'ils aient attiré l'attention de la costumière oscarisée derrière les films Black Panther, Ruth Carter. "C'est tellement génial !!", a-t-elle écrit sur Instagram.

La série d'images, intitulée Fashion Show For Seniors, a suscité des milliers de commentaires similaires.

Avec plus de 100 000 likes pour les photos sur les médias sociaux, le travail d'Afegbua a clairement eu un impact dans le monde réel. Mais des questions subsistent quant à savoir si le travail généré par ordinateur est une menace pour la créativité humaine. Des problèmes éthiques se posent également.

L'artiste, cependant, adopte une approche réfléchie et nuancée.

Nous sommes sur le point de commencer l'interview par Zoom, avec Afegbua assis dans son bureau à Lagos, au Nigeria, lorsque son fils de deux ans réclame un peu d'attention.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

"Il est né intelligent et tout ce qu'il fait est très technologique. Il sait déjà utiliser les téléphones portables et les iPads", dit-il fièrement.

Il est évident qu'il transmet son amour de la technologie et de l'art à son fils, mais qu'est-ce qui a poussé ce diplômé d'une école de commerce à se lancer dans une carrière créative ?

"Quelqu'un m'a fait cadeau d'une caméra et c'est là que ça a décollé".

Il est devenu cinéaste et produit désormais des publicités, des films documentaires et des expositions de réalité virtuelle. Il a également embrassé l'émergence de l'IA en tant que nouvelle force motrice dans l'art.

Avec sa série de défilés de mode, il a vu une occasion de contester ce qu'il considère comme la marginalisation des personnes âgées dans la société et a voulu remettre en question les perceptions autour du vieillissement.

"Je n'ai jamais vu de défilé de mode pour les personnes âgées, mais elles existent - alors pourquoi pas ?".

Une objection évidente est qu'il y a de vraies personnes âgées, et de vrais créateurs de mode, qui auraient pu être photographiés dans le monde réel.

Mais pour Afegbua, c'est le message d'aspiration derrière les images qui est crucial.

Il pense qu'elles peuvent faire réfléchir les gens : "Et si nous commencions à faire les choses de cette manière ?".

L'utilisation de l'IA dans l'art a suscité quelques réactions négatives, notamment parce que l'on se demande si les ordinateurs peuvent vraiment reproduire la créativité humaine, mais M. Afegbua considère qu'il s'agit là d'une occasion passionnante pour les artistes d'évoluer.

Le logiciel d'image de l'IA utilise soit des mots clés (appelés invites) suggérés par l'artiste, soit des photos téléchargées, pour créer une image à partir de ces informations.

Ce qu'Afegbua dit faire avec son travail, c'est apprendre à l'IA à devenir plus créative et, en retour, il fait de nouvelles découvertes.

"L'intelligence artificielle apprend de nous et apprend du World Wide Web. J'essaie d'apprendre d'elle aussi. J'essaie d'apprendre comment lui parler, comment mieux communiquer pour obtenir des résultats exacts de sa part."

Pour les photos du défilé de mode pour les personnes âgées, Afegbua a fait des allers-retours avec plusieurs générateurs d'images IA - il en utilise trois différents pour obtenir des résultats variés - afin de trouver un look qui convienne parfaitement à ses "modèles".

"Je suis un amoureux de la mode, et j'aime toujours expérimenter. Je voulais mélanger la mode traditionnelle africaine nigériane avec quelque chose de futuriste, d'afro-futuriste."

Une autre série de photos, qu'il appelle sa série Fiction, s'inspire également d'une idée du futur - bien que datant le monde qu'il a créé à 250 000 ans.

Galvanisée par les styles de l'armée du Wakanda de Black Panther et de sa nouvelle amie d'Hollywood, Ruth Carter, la collection d'images représente le peuple de Ngochola, une ancienne civilisation africaine imaginée.

"Ils peuvent parler aux machines avec leur esprit parce qu'ils ont déchiffré différents codes. Ils sont très avancés technologiquement dans le sens où ils comprennent comment mélanger la biologie avec, vous savez, la technologie, et les combiner ensemble", dit-il à propos des personnes qui vivent à Ngochola.

Il est clair qu'Afegbua est un défenseur inconditionnel de l'utilisation de l'IA dans l'art, mais il reconnaît que les préoccupations relatives à son utilisation peuvent être valables.

Récemment, des plaintes ont été déposées selon lesquelles les œuvres originales d'artistes sont utilisées sans reconnaissance comme matériau de base, puis manipulées.

Ce n'est pas la méthode d'Afegbua, mais il sait que l'IA peut être utilisée de cette manière.

"En ce qui concerne l'IA, il y a beaucoup de problèmes éthiques liés au fait qu'elle vole le travail d'autres personnes pour créer des tas de choses différentes", admet-il. "C'est un outil - et tout outil peut être utilisé de manière contraire à l'éthique".

La demande d'images générées par l'IA ne semble pas faiblir, le hashtag #AIfilter ayant accumulé 1,3 milliard de vues sur TikTok, où les utilisateurs ont téléchargé des selfies en échange d'une nouvelle image d'eux-mêmes générée par ordinateur.

Afegbua est un optimiste lorsqu'il s'agit de l'utilisation de la technologie dans l'art.

"Je ne pense pas que la technologie ait une durée de vie limitée. Je pense que ça ne peut que s'améliorer, car les algorithmes s'améliorent sans cesse. Les moteurs s'améliorent sans cesse.

"J'ai le sentiment que cela va contribuer à façonner la narration et l'image intentionnelle de l'Afrique maintenant, parce que cela rend les choses beaucoup plus accessibles."

Dans cette optique, Afegbua prévoit de poursuivre le développement de la série Elder.

Il veut utiliser la technologie de l'IA pour aider à réimaginer ce qui est possible aujourd'hui et dans le futur.

Toutes les images sont la propriété de Malik Afegbua/SlickCity.

#5487. Любовники занялись сексом на глазах у десятков свидетелей

В Ирландии любовники занялись сексом в отеле на глазах у десятков свидетелей. Об этом пишет Daily Star.

Мужчину и женщину, предающихся любовным утехам у панорамного окна в пятизвездочном отеле The Marker в Дублине, заметили сотрудники офисного здания напротив. Полностью обнаженная женщина прижалась передней частью тела к стеклу, а мужчина находился сзади. Увидеть происходящее могли не только люди в здании напротив, но и любой прохожий, который посмотрел бы на отель.

Вскоре видеозаписи пары начали распространяться в мессенджерах. Сотрудники офисов заявили, что были не в восторге от этого зрелища. При этом до сих пор неясно, были ли любовники постояльцами гостиницы, так как некоторые номера резервируются для сотрудников. По данным Daily Star, инцидент произошел во время рабочей недели с 19 по 23 октября. Пытается ли полиция ирландской столицы установить личности нарушителей спокойствия, не сообщается.

Ранее сообщалось, что в Великобритании арестовали любовников, которые занялись сексом на глазах у прохожих. Прохожие пожаловались в полицию на мужчину и женщину, которые занимались сексом в центре города Скарборо, графство Норт-Йоркшир.

#5489. Forty Iranian sailors rescued off Sri Lanka coast after medical emergencies

Sri Lanka's foreign ministry says it has coordinated efforts to treat and repatriate 40 Iranian sailors suffering from unspecified medical emergencies in international waters off the island's southeastern coast.

Ministry spokesperson Thushara Rodrigo told BBC Sinhala they received a distress call on Saturday from Iranian ships "regarding an urgent medical need".

The rescue operation was planned by the Iranian Embassy in Colombo, he said.

Iranian ships have been stranded at sea due to a US naval blockade. Sri Lanka stresses it is neutral in the conflict, but has at times offered help to Iranian sailors in what it says is an obligation to international law.

A BBC Sinhala report last month found that there were 21 Iranian vessels located in international waters near Sri Lanka.

The 40 rescued sailors served on different ships - though Sri Lankan authorities do not have information on how many ships they belonged to, Rodrigo said.

The sailors were brought ashore and taken to Colombo for medical treatment before being sent back to Iran by plane on Saturday night, he added.

He said that several agencies were involved in the operation, including local shipping companies.

According to Rodrigo, Sri Lanka was obliged under international law and humanitarian grounds to provide the necessary facilities for medical emergencies.

"This does not mean that we will provide assistance to those ships," he said. "It is generally an internationally accepted tradition to respond to a distress call after receiving it."

"We have dealt with such cases before. This is a normal process that continues to be implemented."

The ongoing conflict in Iran started when the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on the country in February. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.

Attacks by both sides have persisted as negotiations stalled.

Sri Lanka has sought to remain neutral in the conflict, having rejected military access requests from both the US and Iran and urged both parties to prioritise dialogue.

It has also offered assistance to Iranian ships caught in the conflict on what it argues are humanitarian grounds.

In March, Sri Lankan authorities said they responded to a distress call from the Iranian ship the Iris Dena, which had sunk off its coast after a US torpedo attack.

More than 80 crew members were killed in the attack, and injured survivors were taken to a hospital in the Galle Harbour.

The following day, Sri Lankan authorities allowed another Iranian naval vessel to dock at one of its ports, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake saying that they would "never hesitate to protect humanity".

Sri Lankan authorities said earlier this month they had no immediate plans to send aid to 19 Iranian ships near its coasts which had reported shortages of food, water and fuel. The authorities said they had to prioritise national interests, the Associated Press reported.

Die Regisseurin, Drehbuchautorin und Lehrende Olga Kosanovic mit ihrem Buchtipp.

Bevor ich die österreichische Staatsbürgerschaft bekomme, muss ich die serbische zurücklegen." #5491. Singapore’s estimated geothermal resource potential more than 60 times annual electricity consumption: EMA

A non-invasive geophysical survey found high-temperature geothermal resources several kilometres underground that may be suitable for electricity generation.

Visitors having a foot bath at the new Sembawang Hot Spring Park on Jan 4, 2020. (Photo: CNA/Jeremy Long)

SINGAPORE: Singapore's geothermal resource potential is estimated to be more than 60 times its annual electricity consumption, according to preliminary findings from a survey, the Energy Market Authority (EMA) said on Monday (Oct 26).

The non-invasive geophysical survey, conducted from 2024 to 2026, found high-temperature geothermal resources several kilometres underground that may be suitable for electricity generation. Singapore's current annual electricity consumption is around 60 terawatt-hours.

Further studies will be needed to validate the estimates of Singapore's geothermal technical potential and determine how much geothermal energy can be feasibly extracted.

Speaking at the Singapore International Energy Week 2026 on Monday, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng described the findings as "a very good start", adding that if realised, geothermal energy could power Singapore for the next 60 or so years.

The nationwide survey was conducted by a consortium of leading global consultants, including Chevron, Metatek Group, and Surbana Jurong.

It used two non-invasive techniques to develop three-dimensional geological and heat resource models of Singapore.

Metatek Group undertook the data acquisition and processing, while Chevron used the processed data to develop a 3D geological and heat resource model of Singapore.

The survey assessed geothermal resources at depths of up to 10km for the purpose of power generation.

The consortium also assessed that there are lower-temperature geothermal resources at shallower depths, which could potentially support industrial heating and cooling using heat pumps and absorption chillers.

CNA Games Guess Word Crack the word, one row at a time Buzzword Create words using the given letters Mini Sudoku Tiny puzzle, mighty brain teaser Mini Crossword Small grid, big challenge Word Search Spot as many words as you can Show More Show Less

Following the preliminary findings, EMA said it would proceed with the next phase of studies to further assess the feasibility of harnessing geothermal energy for electricity generation, cooling and heating.

It has appointed a consortium formed by Surbana Jurong and GLJ Ltd to study the potential deployment of next-generation geothermal plants in Singapore.

The study will cover safety considerations, technical viability and the cost of geothermal energy production. It is scheduled to start by the end of this year and is estimated to take around 15 months.

Dr Tan noted that the process would not be straightforward, referring to how geothermal resources are located several kilometres underground.

The amount of electricity that can eventually be generated will depend on the cost and technical feasibility of extracting these resources, as well as the pace of advances in deep drilling technology, Dr Tan said.

"Our dense urban environment will also affect how many geothermal power plants we can eventually or feasibly deploy, and most importantly, we must keep safety as a top-of-mind consideration," he added.

EMA chief executive Puah Kok Keong said geothermal energy was an "indigenous source of clean energy that can provide constant power, and can potentially play an important role in our energy mix".

"If proven to be viable for electricity generation, Singapore’s geothermal energy resources will strengthen our energy resilience and support the decarbonisation of the power sector,” he added.

Dr Tan said that Singapore has not made a decision on whether to deploy geothermal power.

"It could take many years before we get to that decision. But nevertheless, as I've said many times before, no option is off the table for us here in Singapore. We will therefore explore this option seriously," he added.

Large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport, in Riyadh. Image used for representation purpose only. | Photo Credit: Reuters

The Saudi-led military coalition said on Monday (October 26, 2026) it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis, after the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on the international airport in Riyadh.

The operation came a day after explosions rattled the Saudi capital and authorities sent text messages to residents warning them of a “hostile aerial threat” targeting the city.

The Houthis have carried out waves of strikes on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and injured more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said on Monday (October 26, 2026) that air defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile” fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh, and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Yemen’s capital Sanaa.

“We continue the process of dismantling the ballistic missile network of the terrorist Houthi militia,” Al-Malki wrote on X.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Monday the group “successfully targeted” the airport with a ballistic missile, and struck oil pumping stations with drones.

“The Yemeni Armed Forces carried out two qualitative military operations targeting the Saudi enemy troop concentrations and weapons depots” in the Aden and Lahj governorates in Yemen, which caused “dozens of casualties”, Saree added.

On Sunday (October 25, 2026), the Houthis said they had launched an attack on the airport in Riyadh, after the kingdom announced that flights had resumed.

The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, forcing the postponement of the kingdom’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.

The Dakar Rally also joined a growing list of events that were cancelled, postponed or relocated amid the fallout from the war.

Saree had earlier warned that Riyadh airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target”, and urged airlines and travellers to avoid it.

“The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport,” the spokesman said.

Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer, shifting the focus of the wider US-Iran war that erupted in February.

As operations resumed at Riyadh airport, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis met Saudi de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

During the meeting, Mitsotakis “responded favourably to the kingdom’s request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances”, his office said.

Greece has deployed a battery to operate the US-made Patriot air defence system in Yanbu, a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast.

On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said it intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.

“The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning -- may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions,” one resident in Saudi Arabia’s Khamis Mushait told AFP on Sunday (October 25, 2026) on condition of anonymity.

The kingdom’s civil defence agency later said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles.

Images released by the SPA showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road.

#5496. Nager avec des prédateurs marins - le photographe qui a réalisé son "rêve fou"

"La peur me fait rester vigilant, elle ne m'a pas empêché de faire quoi que ce soit", déclare Amos Nachoum, un photographe animalier de renommée internationale pour ses images sous-marines.

De l'Antarctique au Haut-Arctique, il a plongé dans des environnements extrêmes pour capturer certains des prédateurs les plus magnifiques et les plus insaisissables qui vivent sous l'eau.

Parmi les nombreuses créatures qu'il a photographiées, la liste comprend des baleines bleues, des orques, des anacondas, des crocodiles du Nil et, bien sûr, des requins.

Mais contrairement à la plupart des photographes, Amos n'utilise pas de cage de sécurité dans l'eau.

"Je voulais montrer en image, ce qu'il faut faire pour traiter avec le Grand Blanc", explique-t-il à l'émission de radio Outlook de la BBC.

"Si nous ne le taquinons pas, si nous ne l'aggravons pas, nous pouvons être avec eux de manière pacifique".

En fait, il n'était qu'à un mètre de lui lorsqu'il a pris des photos d'un grand requin blanc.

Nous sommes habitués à voir les mâchoires d'un requin comme un symbole de terreur.

Mais le photographe israélien voit l'élégance, la puissance et la beauté de l'animal.

Depuis 45 ans, il dit s'efforcer de changer l'idée fausse et répandue selon laquelle certaines espèces, comme le grand blanc, ne sont que des machines à tuer sans pitié.

"Il n'y a pas de démons en mer", dit-il souvent.

Aujourd'hui considéré comme l'un des meilleurs photographes dans son domaine et titulaire de nombreux prix, Amos Nachoom a eu son premier contact avec un appareil photo à l'adolescence, lorsqu'il en a trouvé un par hasard dans la réserve de son père à l'âge de douze ans.

Il vivait à Tel Aviv avec ses parents, un couple juif qui avait fui la Libye.

Amos a appris à se servir d'un vieil appareil et a commencé à prendre des photos.

"Je me suis rendu compte que la photographie me donnait une chance de m'exprimer", se souvient-il.

Sa relation avec son père, qu'il décrit comme un homme strict et discipliné, était difficile.

Il a quitté la maison à l'âge de 14 ans pour vivre et travailler avec les pêcheurs locaux, qui lui ont enseigné une compétence essentielle, la plongée.

Plus tard, alors qu'il était jeune homme, il a effectué son service militaire, qui est obligatoire en Israël, et a combattu lors de la guerre israélo-arabe de 1973.

Amos dit avoir été traumatisé par la violence et il a quitté Israël pour commencer une nouvelle vie aux États-Unis.

Il a conduit des taxis à New York et a gagné sa vie en faisant des petits boulots, avant de trouver sa place dans l'eau - en tant que moniteur de plongée.

Alors qu'il accompagnait un groupe de touristes en vacances de plongée, un vieil Américain prenant des photos avec un appareil photo sous-marin lui a donné une idée.

Une fois qu'il a combiné la plongée avec la photographie, il a entrepris d'apporter un regard nouveau sur les grandes créatures qui se cachent sous la mer.

"Le rapport aux grands animaux, aux requins et aux baleines, était très négatif", se souvient-il, "mais mon rapport était très positif".

Amos avait un rêve particulier qu'il voulait réaliser : devenir le premier homme à photographier un ours polaire - dans l'eau.

Il se souvient que son père l'a qualifié de "mission suicide" lorsqu'il a entendu parler de ses projets.

"Il y avait une déconnexion totale", dit Amos à propos de son père, qui aurait préféré le voir s'installer et se marier.

"Il a renoncé à moi. Il ne pouvait pas se connecter à ce que je faisais".

Sans se décourager, Amos s'est rendu dans l'Arctique au printemps 2000.

Avec l'aide d'un guide inuit local, il a repéré un ours polaire mâle et a plongé dans l'eau.

"Il faut toujours un très bon guide et beaucoup d'expérience avant de faire quelque chose comme ça, car il y a une chance qu'il y ait un accident".

Le vent poussait leur bateau loin d'Amos, alors que l'ours polaire ne cessait de se rapprocher.

Mais Amos avait fait ses devoirs à l'avance. Il avait lu que les ours polaires ne pouvaient pas plonger au-delà de 10 mètres de profondeur.

"L'ours polaire est très lourd et a beaucoup de graisse dans son corps et sa fourrure. Il doit travailler très dur pour descendre", explique-t-il.

Des décennies d'expérience lui ont appris à rechercher les signes chez un animal qui pourraient indiquer qu'une attaque est imminente.

Lorsque l'ours est arrivé à près de six mètres de lui, Amos a plongé, l'ours le suivant.

"J'étais à environ 15 à 17 mètres et il continuait à descendre. Je ne pouvais voir que les pattes de sa main, son nez et son museau. Honnêtement, j'ai eu peur."

Amos a eu peu de chance de se battre ou de fuir le grand carnivore.

"Quand j'étais à environ 75 pieds, j'ai levé les yeux. Au lieu de faire face verticalement à moi, l'ours était plus horizontal et nageait avec le niveau de l'eau."

Il a survécu, et heureusement, lorsqu'il est remonté à la surface, l'ours polaire avait disparu.

Un voyage dans l'Arctique coûte beaucoup d'argent et de préparation, notamment la location d'un avion charter et le montage de tentes.

Amos était déterminé à essayer une deuxième fois de prendre la photo de ses rêves.

L'occasion s'est présentée des années plus tard, lorsque son élève Yonatan Mir a réalisé un film documentaire sur lui, emmenant les deux hommes dans les étendues sauvages de l'Arctique en 2015.

Un budget d'un million de dollars (614 185 160 FCFA) a été obtenu pour le projet, une somme qui leur permettrait de rester cinq jours seulement.

Ils ont cherché pendant quatre jours sans aucune chance, jusqu'à ce que le moment joyeux arrive.

"Nous les avons vus descendre la colline et entrer dans l'eau."

Ils avaient enfin repéré une mère ourse avec ses deux oursons.

Photographier un ours polaire avec deux oursons serait une première pour un photographe.

Cette fois, Amos Nachoum avait un partenaire de plongée, Adam, qui était là pour filmer l'événement.

"Ils se sont approchés de plus en plus près et directement vers nous. J'ai regardé Adam et j'ai retiré le détendeur de ma bouche, j'ai souri et remis le détendeur et je suis descendu", se souvient Amos.

"Elle (l'ours polaire) est passée au-dessus de notre tête. Je me suis retourné sur le ventre pour prendre une photo d'elle. "

L'image qu'il a prise était la silhouette d'un ours, il a donc attendu le cliché montrant les ours le regardant fixement.

"La mère ourse était d'abord au-dessus de l'eau. Puis elle a mis sa tête en bas. Je cliquais, autant de photos que je pouvais prendre."

Alors qu'Amos zoomait sur les ours polaires, les réalisateurs du documentaire ont parlé à son père, qui est maintenant alité, de retour en Israël.

Il a décrit Amos comme "mon bon garçon, mon fils fou et mon héros".

Pendant la majeure partie de sa vie d'adulte, Amos dit qu'il a à peine parlé à son père.

"J'étais abasourdi. J'avais du mal à comprendre ce qui sortait de sa bouche et à savoir ce qu'il pensait de moi."

Son père est décédé avant qu'Amos puisse retourner en Israël.

Mais à son retour, il s'est rendu au cimetière, emportant avec lui la photo encadrée de l'ours polaire pour la placer sur la tombe de son père.

"J'ai réalisé quelque chose qu'il ne pensait pas que je puisse faire".

Mais le célèbre photographe ajoute également .

"Il m'a mis au défi d'être le meilleur que je puisse être".

#5497. Раскрыт неожиданный способ борьбы с дефицитом витамина D

Фото: New Africa / Shutterstock / Fotodom

Регулярная физическая активность может помогать поддерживать уровень витамина D в организме даже без приема специальных добавок. К такому выводу пришли британские ученые, чья работа опубликована в Frontiers in Endocrinology.

Авторы научного обзора проанализировали результаты исследований, посвященных влиянию физических нагрузок на обмен витамина D. Ранее основными способами борьбы с его недостатком считались изменение питания и прием добавок.

Выяснилось, что даже одна тренировка способна временно повышать концентрацию витамина D и его активной формы в крови. Такие изменения наблюдались уже в течение нескольких часов после физической нагрузки.

При этом регулярные занятия спортом давали более продолжительный эффект. Исследования показали, что физическая активность замедляла естественное снижение уровня витамина D в зимние месяцы, даже если участники не теряли вес.

Более того, у регулярно тренировавшихся людей не наблюдалось сезонного снижения концентрации биологически активной формы витамина D, которая участвует в регуляции различных процессов в организме.

Ученые подчеркнули, что физическая активность влияет на обмен витамина D не только в краткосрочной, но и в долгосрочной перспективе. По их мнению, регулярные тренировки могут стать дополнительным способом профилактики его недостатка. При этом авторы не предлагают полностью заменять физическими нагрузками витаминные добавки.

Ранее стало известно, что экстракт виноградных косточек и витамин B9 могут снижать жесткость артерий.

#5499. A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?

Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canal

As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.

He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.

South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.

With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.

The first task was to determine the species.

Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.

The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.

The dusky shark was first spotted in the canal in mid-September

A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.

They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.

Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.

As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.

Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".

People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.

Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.

City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.

A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.

Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.

Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.

A poster encourages support for a baseball stadium "on behalf of Bukangi"

More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.

The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.

"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for herâ¦ It's a lot of fun."

But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.

As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.

Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.

Kim Joo-eun and her nieces were among Bukangi's many visitors

At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.

But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.

On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.

At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.

The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.

It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.

The canal leading up to the Busan port where Bukangi was stranded

With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.

On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".

When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"

"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."

Jeong protesting against Bukangi's "eviction", alongside a man demanding officials "protect Bukangi's right to self-determination"

Others thought it was time for her to return home.

"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."

People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.

"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."

Bukangi became a sensation, drawing the curious and the concerned

Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.

"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."

Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.

On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.

This left her trapped between the two layers.

Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.

Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.

Staying in the canal is dangerous for Bukangi, says marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo

There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.

Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.

She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.

But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.

For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.

Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

#5502. Bank of Japan's hawkish pause to leave scope for December hike

FILE PHOTO: Traffic signs in front of the Bank of Japan building in Tokyo, Japan, June 15, 2026. REUTERS/Kim Kyung-Hoon/File Photo

TOKYO, Oct 26 : The Bank of Japan will likely declare victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its 2 per cent inflation target at its policy meeting on Friday and emphasise the risks prices could overshoot, signaling the chance of a rate hike as soon as December.

Such hawkish language may reinforce expectations the BOJ, US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank will all raise rates by year-end, as brisk AI demand and the Iran war-induced energy shock worsen global inflationary pressures.

Still, the BOJ is likely to avoid dropping explicit hints on the timing and pace of future rate rises as it balances the need to forestall risks of an inflation overshoot without disrupting jittery markets with a premature hike, analysts say.

"With rises in prices and wages moderate, the BOJ will keep raising rates gradually without rushing," said a person familiar with its thinking, a view echoed by two more people.

At the two-day policy meeting ending on Friday, the BOJ is set to maintain its policy rate at 1.25 per cent by a majority vote, forgoing a back-to-back hike to spend more time scrutinising the effect of past rate hikes on lending conditions.

In a quarterly report due after the meeting, the BOJ is likely to slightly revise up next fiscal year's price forecast and signal that underlying inflation has roughly achieved its 2 per cent target, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters.

With wage gains becoming embedded and inflation expectations hovering around 2 per cent, the central bank will likely stress that it will now focus on anchoring inflation around its target by raising rates toward levels deemed neutral to the economy.

While Governor Kazuo Ueda has already signaled such a shift in policy focus upon raising rates in September, the pivot would mark another symbolic departure from the BOJ's prolonged efforts to fire up inflation through ultra-loose monetary policy.

"It's a historical moment for the BOJ, though it faces a more challenging task now that it needs to step not just on the accelerator but the brakes," said Naomi Muguruma, chief bond strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities.

"The BOJ will probably scrutinise upcoming data and market moves in deciding whether to raise rates in December, or hold until January," she said.

Analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.5 per cent in December and stick to a quarterly pace of rate hikes.

Under former governor Haruhiko Kuroda, the BOJ deployed a massive stimulus in 2013 to pull Japan out of deflation and fire up inflation to its 2 per cent inflation target.

Even after ending its mix of unorthodox easing steps in 2024, the central bank has trodden cautiously in raising rates on the view underlying inflation - or price moves excluding one-off factors and driven by domestic demand - remained below target.

With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised rates in September after delivering a hike in June - a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025.

The BOJ's policy rate, at 1.25 per cent, is now within the range of 1.1 per cent to 2.5 per cent its staff estimated as Japan's neutral rate, or the level that neither cools nor overheats the economy - drawing market attention to how far it could eventually hike rates.

With growth in bank lending still strong, the central bank is likely to stress on Friday that financial conditions remain loose - signalling scope for further rate hikes before its policy rate reaches levels close to neutral, the people said.

The BOJ's meeting follows that of the Fed, which is seen skipping a hike at its two-day meeting concluding on Wednesday. The ECB is also set to keep rates unchanged at 2.5 per cent on Thursday.

Published - October 26, 2026 09:27 am IST - JERUSALEM/LONDON

Representational image. | Photo Credit: Getty Images/iStockphoto

Israel's markets have soared despite three years of war and political turmoil, but ​some investors see further upside if the Opposition defeats Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday’s (October 27, 2026) election, potentially easing regional tensions and political risk.

Opinion polls point to a ‌tight contest, with neither Mr. Netanyahu's ruling Likud bloc nor an opposition alliance centred on former military chief Gadi Eisenkot expected ​to secure the 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset needed to govern.

That raises the prospect of lengthy coalition negotiations or even ⁠another election. Since the October 7 Hamas attacks in 2023, the Tel Aviv stock market has soared 130%, far outpacing Wall Street's 80% gain, while the shekel has climbed 25%, one of the world's strongest currency performances.

Analysts attribute some of that strength to Israel's tech sector and the global AI boom, while defence spending, which ‌has nearly doubled to around 8% of GDP, has also provided a boost.

With both Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Eisenkot vowing to maintain pressure on Hamas and Iran, markets are focused on their broader policy differences. JPMorgan estimates the shekel could swing as much as ‌3% depending on the result.

An opposition victory that improves relations with Western allies and halts a judicial overhaul that sparked mass protests in ‌2023 ⁠could strengthen the currency, JPMorgan said, while another Netanyahu-led government could weaken it.

Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, while stopping short of backing ⁠a candidate, said a government without far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich would signal that Israel was "turning a new page”, potentially helping rebuild its international credibility and expand the Abraham Accords with its neighbours.

IBI Investment House also expects an Opposition victory to lift the markets. "From a capital markets perspective, this would likely be reflected in a decline in Israel's risk ​premium, appreciation pressure on the shekel, and a positive reaction in the ‌local market," IBI's Chief Economist Rafi Gozlan said.

"The most significant issue is what the result will mean for the region," said Equity Bank's chief economic adviser Charlie Robertson. "If Netanyahu is reelected it might increase the chances of further escalation with Iran, whereas a defeat might be seen as lessening the tensions."

But the prospect of gains under an Opposition government does not mean investors expect Israeli assets to suffer if Mr. Netanyahu ‌remains in power. Stocks and bonds have proved remarkably resilient through years of war and political upheaval, and some investors remain confident ​in the economy regardless of the election outcome.

Union Investment's Sergey Dergachev has been buying Israeli bonds ahead of the election, betting the economy and companies he favours will remain fundamentally strong. "We are very constructive on Israeli credits going into the election," Mr. Dergachev ⁠said, adding that bonds were less prone to major swings and the region's intertwined conflicts should eventually ease.

Despite the rally, foreign investors remain cautious. Copley Fund Research data show the share of global funds holding Israeli equities is at a record low, having fallen sharply since 2023.

T. S. Lombard's Christopher Granville cited ‌central bank estimates that the war had cost the economy more than $55 billion by last year, equivalent to 8.6% in cumulative lost GDP growth.

Israel's fiscal position is another focus. Public debt has risen to nearly 70% of GDP, around 10 percentage points higher than in 2022, while the budget deficit is expected to remain around 4.5% of GDP, versus less than 2% before the conflict.

Central bank head Amir Yaron stressed last week the need to "preserve adequate fiscal policy space" given the Iran war.

Like stocks, Israeli government bonds have rallied, returning about 30% over the last two years, more than double the main emerging market indexes.

The main risk for investors is an inconclusive result that prolongs political uncertainty, delaying budgets, reforms and investment, some investors ‌believe.

That uncertainty can produce sharp short-term swings. Tel Aviv Stock Exchange research covering the last 10 elections found volatility in leading share indexes rose by as much as ​45% in the weeks after voting compared with a typical week. But initial losses were typically recovered within a month, with the indexes posting an average gain of about 1.7%.

Over a longer horizon, the TA-125 returned an average 16.4% in the year ⁠following elections, compared with a long-term annual average of 11.5%, the research found. Political deadlock often weighed on stocks before voting, but the effects typically faded within months, ⁠said Nissan Avraham, an analyst at the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's research unit.

That record supports the view that elections matter less for Israeli companies than many investors assume.

Lior Yochpaz, chief investment officer at insurance company Menora Mivtachim, said businesses have continued to thrive despite ‌years of political upheaval, judicial overhaul proposals and regional conflict, helped by a relatively business-friendly environment.

For some investors, however, the more attractive election trade lies outside Israel. TT International's Jean-Charles Sambor said an Opposition victory or weakened Netanyahu government could ease regional tensions and benefit Lebanese bonds.

"The best way ​to play it for us is through other West Asia countries, and for us Lebanon is a good proxy," Mr. Sambor said.

#5507. «Объясняю для дураков». Маск обвинил Киев в нарушении условий использования Starlink. Он привел в доказательство пост Зеленского

Основатель компании SpaceX Илон Маск ответил на критику ограничения работы спутниковой системы связи Starlink для Вооруженных сил Украины (ВСУ). Он привел в пример заявление президента Украины Владимира Зеленского. По словам Маска, глава республики сам подтвердил, что гражданскую систему использовали для наступательных операций.

Объясняю для дураков: Зеленский сам разместил пост об использовании Starlink для нанесения ударов беспилотниками, что всегда противоречило условиям предоставления услуг

По его словам, если система спутниковой связи Starlink будет служить не только гражданским целям, возникнет риск ответных ударов по ней. «Это действительно одна из главных причин, по которой Starlink должна оставаться гражданской операцией», — заявил миллиардер.

Маск добавил, что систему можно применять для создания военной инфраструктуры, но не для нанесения наступательных ударов, из-за которых Starlink превратилась бы в законную цель для ответной атаки.

Если бы противник взорвал спутники Starlink, это привело бы к разрушительному эффекту домино, который вызвал бы образование обширного поля обломков, делающих космос непригодным для использования

В Киеве отвергли обвинения американского миллиардера в нарушении условий использования Starlink, пишет The Washington Post. По словам источника издания в офисе президента Украины, SpaceX не связывалась с представителями администрации по поводу этих обвинений.

Советник украинского лидера по вопросам оборонных технологий Сергей Бескрестнов (Флэш) выразил недоумение по поводу того, что предприниматель оказался не в курсе ограничений работы Starlink на Украине. Он подчеркнул, что в стране с февраля 2026 года действуют ограничения скорости терминалов, из-за которых ВСУ не могли использовать коммерческие спутники для нанесения ударов с помощью дипстрайков и мидлстрайков.

По словам экс-советника министра обороны Украины по вопросам использования БПЛА на фронте Сергея Стерненко, дроны передвигаются на скорости от 120 километров в час, а Starlink переставала работать уже на скорости 60-70 километров в час. Он пояснил, что, таким образом, для всего, что движется быстрее, применялась военная система Starshield.

Иными словами, использование гражданской версии Starlink для выполнения задач с применением дронов было технически невозможно. Все миссии дронов, требующие спутниковой связи, могли осуществляться только с помощью Starshield

Маск ранее заявил, что линия фронта Вооруженных сил Украины обрушится в случае отключения спутниковой связи Starlink. По его словам, обвал произойдет немедленно.

Миллиардер добавил, что Starlink критически важна для обороны Украины.

Директор по военному анализу американского исследовательского центра Defense Priorities Дженнифер Кавана отметил, что ограничение работы спутниковой связи Starlink может существенно снизить боеспособность ВСУ. Он отметил, что перебои в работе системы способны нарушить использование беспилотников и осложнить оборону позиций на передовой.

По словам эксперта, проблемы со спутниковой связью могут затруднить наведение на цели, так как украинские военные используют системы Starlink и Starshield для получения информации в режиме реального времени.

#5508. Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado makes surprise return home after nearly a year abroad

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado joins Rachel Campos-Duffy in Panama to warn Americans about the dangers of socialism ahead of the midterms. Machado shares a direct message to President Donald Trump, praising his leadership and stating that capturing Maduro would be his legacy. She also criticizes Delcy Rodriguez over the response to devastating earthquakes in Venezuela.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado made returned to her home country on Sunday after nearly a year abroad, re-entering a political landscape transformed by the U.S. ouster of Nicolás Maduro.

"I'm here. With you all," Machado wrote on social media, announcing her return for the first time since December. Her homecoming comes as Venezuela remains under the leadership of acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a longtime Maduro ally backed by the Trump administration, with no presidential election scheduled.

President Donald Trump, asked about Machado's return by reporters in Port Huron, Michigan, said he was unaware of the development but expressed hope for her safety.

TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado arrives at a church after returning to the country following nearly a year abroad, in Lara, Venezuela, Oct. 25, 2026. (Vente Venezuela Press/Handout via REUTERS)

"I don't know anything about it, but I think she's a very nice woman," Trump said. "She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe. She's a very nice woman. But we're doing really well in Venezuela."

Machado presented the Nobel Peace Prize she won to President Trump last week. (White House handout via Reuters)

Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025 for her peaceful opposition to Maduro's government, did not disclose her exact location or provide details about how she returned.

Fellow opposition leader Edmundo González, who ran for president in 2024 after Machado was barred from seeking office, confirmed her arrival on social media and said he would join her "very soon."

"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González wrote on X. "You know it, this is until the end."

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado speaks during a news conference at The Heritage Foundation in Washington, DC, on Jan. 16, 2026. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Machado's return comes nearly 10 months after U.S. forces captured Maduro in January, removing the longtime leader from power.

Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice president, has remained in power with the Trump administration's support, despite exceeding the period she was initially authorized to serve as acting president.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado displays vote tally sheets during a protest against the reelection of President Nicolás Maduro one month after the disputed presidential vote which she says the opposition won by a landslide, in Caracas, Venezuela, Wednesday, Aug. 28, 2024. (Cristian Hernandez/AP Photo)

Trump has repeatedly praised his administration's relationship with Rodríguez, highlighting agreements involving Venezuelan oil production and other business ventures with American companies.

NICOLAS MADURO AND WIFE CILIA FLORES FACE NEW CHARGES OF CONSPIRACY TO TORTURE AMERICANS

In September, Trump said it was too soon to consider holding democratic elections in Venezuela, with U.S. officials prioritizing economic stabilization. Machado and her allies, meanwhile, have pushed for an election date, arguing that democratic governance is essential to the country's long-term stability.

Her return could complicate relations between the Venezuelan opposition, the interim government and Washington. Reuters reported in June that U.S. officials had asked Machado to delay her return.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gestures at a protest ahead of the Friday inauguration of President Nicolas Maduro for his third term, in Caracas, Venezuela January 9, 2025. (REUTERS/Maxwell Briceno)

Machado spent much of 2025 in hiding after being briefly detained following an opposition protest that January. She later secretly left Venezuela and resurfaced in Norway in December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

Meanwhile, a faction of the Venezuelan opposition and Rodríguez's government held another round of talks this month focused on reforms to the country's Supreme Court and electoral authorities ahead of eventual elections, Reuters reported.

Machado's political movement has not participated in those negotiations.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

#5512. Simba faces possible fines, licence cancellation over allegations of intentional spectrum misuse

Simba's unauthorised spectrum use was allegedly intentional and approved by senior management. The telco is also accused of deliberately failing to fully comply with an order to produce documents.

A Simba shop at Canberra Plaza in Singapore on Aug 18, 2025. (Photo: CNA/Ooi Boon Keong)

SINGAPORE: Telecommunications operator Simba could face fines, suspension or cancellation of its licence over alleged unauthorised spectrum use and other regulatory breaches, according to new details of an ongoing investigation disclosed by its Australian parent company Tuas on Monday (Oct 26).

In a filing to the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX), Tuas said the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) had issued Simba a notice to show cause, setting out six allegations involving unauthorised spectrum use, breaches of telecommunications regulations and concerns about the company's governance and compliance practices.

These include allegations that Simba's unauthorised use of radio frequency bands was intentional and approved by its senior management, and that the telco deliberately failed to fully comply with an order to produce documents.

The filing also outlined potential regulatory actions being considered by IMDA, including financial penalties and the suspension or cancellation of Simba's spectrum rights or telecommunications licence.

CNA Games Guess Word Crack the word, one row at a time Buzzword Create words using the given letters Mini Sudoku Tiny puzzle, mighty brain teaser Mini Crossword Small grid, big challenge Word Search Spot as many words as you can Show More Show Less IMDA previously disclosed in May that it was investigating Simba over possible unauthorised spectrum use, prompting it to suspend its review of the telco's proposed S$1.43 billion (US$1.11 billion) acquisition of rival operator M1. The deal was subsequently terminated.

IMDA previously disclosed in May that it was investigating Simba over possible unauthorised spectrum use, prompting it to suspend its review of the telco's proposed S$1.43 billion (US$1.11 billion) acquisition of rival operator M1.

According to Monday's filing, IMDA alleged that Simba deployed dynamic spectrum sharing technology at about 133 sites for intermittent periods in 2022 and 2023.

This allowed the telco to use the 2100 megahertz (MHz) frequency band for both 4G and 5G services, even though it was authorised to use the band only for 5G.

Dynamic spectrum sharing is a technology that allows different generations of mobile networks, such as 4G and 5G, to share the same frequency band.

IMDA also alleged that Simba used spectrum in the 2340MHz to 2360MHz band at about 92 sites for intermittent periods between 2023 and 2026, despite not having authorisation to do so.

The regulator alleged that both instances of unauthorised spectrum use were intentional and approved by Simba's senior management.

Separately, IMDA alleged that Simba deployed 5G indoor radio access network equipment at two locations in 2023 before receiving authorisation to do so. Approval was only granted on Nov 14 that year.

The regulator also alleged that Simba did not fully comply with an order to produce documents, and that its failure to do so was deliberate and intentional.

IMDA further raised concerns about deficiencies in Simba's governance and compliance culture, which it considers should be addressed through additional regulatory obligations.

IMDA could impose financial penalties of up to 10 per cent of the annual turnover of the relevant part of Simba's business or S$1 million, whichever is higher.

Other possible actions include suspending or cancelling Simba's spectrum rights or telecommunications licence, shortening its licence period, or imposing additional regulatory obligations to address governance deficiencies.

Simba has until Nov 16 to respond to the show cause notice.

Tuas noted that IMDA has not reached any conclusions on whether regulatory action should be taken against Simba or what form such action might take.

"Simba intends to respond to the Show Cause Notice," the company said.

"As the matter remains under consideration by the regulator and no findings have been made or confirmed, Tuas does not intend to provide further comment on the matters raised in this announcement."

IMDA first disclosed its investigation into Simba in May, saying it had uncovered possible unauthorised spectrum use by the telco.

The regulator suspended its review of Simba's proposed S$1.43 billion acquisition of M1, saying the findings of its investigation could be material to its assessment of the deal.

The proposed acquisition, which would have consolidated two of Singapore's four mobile network operators, was subsequently terminated after the deadline for its completion passed.

Monday's filing sets out more specific allegations, including that certain instances of unauthorised spectrum use were intentional and approved by senior management.

Radio frequency spectrum refers to the electromagnetic waves used to carry wireless communications, including mobile phone calls and data.

IMDA regulates the allocation and assignment of spectrum to telecommunications operators, which are authorised to use specific frequency bands for their services.

These rules are intended to prevent interference between wireless services and ensure that operators use spectrum in accordance with their assigned rights and licence conditions.

#5513. Leafy spurge may have arrived in North America through a Massachusetts ballast dump in 1827

Leafy spurge is an invasive plant that was first recorded in Newbury, Massachusetts, in 1827. It spread rapidly across the northern United States and southern Canada during the early 1900s. By this time, it was established in several states and regions, including Ontario and Iowa. The plant has significant ecological impacts, often replacing native vegetation and causing issues for grazing animals.

Updated - October 26, 2026 09:08 am IST - PORT HURON

President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at McMorran Place Arena in Port Huron, Mich., October 25, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

President Donald Trump at a Sunday (October 25, 2026) campaign rally ratcheted ‌up his push to link U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim extremists, comparing him to the 9/11 ​attackers while saying Democrats would let violent anti-American terrorists into the United States.

"I'm here to keep a jihadist, ⁠Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator," the President told a receptive audience in Port Huron, which is in a Michigan area where 66% of the vote went to Mr. Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

If Mr. El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. ‌Mr. Trump has sought to paint him as an anti-American Muslim radical, and on Sunday (October 25, 2026) he took the rhetoric to a new level, likening Mr. El-Sayed to the attackers who took over United Flight 93 during the September 11, ‌2001, attacks.

Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive U.S. Senate contests going into the November 3 midterm elections, ‌with former ⁠U.S. Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, and Mr. El-Sayed vying for an open seat that will help to decide ⁠control of the chamber.

The President on Sunday (October 25, 2026) compared voting against Mr. El-Sayed to the actions of Michigan native Todd Beamer and others who fought back against the Flight 93 hijackers.

"Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," said Mr. Trump.

If Mr. El-Sayed ​wins, "he would be the only senator that will have ‌to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go in the Senate," Mr. Trump said.

Mr. El-Sayed has dismissed the accusations against him, and at a Sunday (October 25, 2026) night event, he suggested that Mr. Trump's frequent emphasis of Mr. El-Sayed's name contains a measure of hypocrisy.

"I get that the President of the United States takes personal offence to my first name," Mr. El-Sayed told an audience ‌in Grand Rapids, Michigan. "He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding ​his son-in-law’s private equity, doesn’t seem to mind as much when it’s the Qataris who are giving him a $400 million private jet."

Affinity Partners, Mr. Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner's investment fund, has reportedly received billions from a Saudi Government ⁠entity. Qatar gifted Mr. Trump a Boeing 747 jet.

The mostly White crowd at Sunday's (October 25, 2026) rally cheered Mr. Trump’s comments on Mr. El-Sayed. Some attendees yelled “traitor” and others yelled “deport,” although Mr. El-Sayed was born in Michigan.

Terrance Camburn, a 52-year-old disabled Army veteran from Sandusky, ‌Michigan, said he supported Mr. Trump’s criticism because of Mr. El-Sayed’s “political beliefs.”

“I’ve been down to Dearborn and I’ve seen many of the things he agrees with,” Mr. Camburn said when asked about Mr. Trump’s 9/11 comments.

Dearborn, Michigan, has the highest per-capita concentration of Muslims of any U.S. city.

As he left the venue after the rally, Mr. Rogers did not respond to Reuters' questions about Mr. Trump's invocation of 9/11. But earlier on Sunday (October 25, 2026), he said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he did not agree with the notion that Mr. El-Sayed is a violent terrorist.

"I've never called him a terrorist," Mr. Rogers told NBC.

Mr. Rogers has alleged without evidence that Mr. El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the ‌Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

Mr. El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood, saying it is "shameful" for Mr. Rogers to question his allegiance to the ​United States.

Mr. Rogers told "Meet the Press" that Mr. El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about the allegations.

"He's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America," he said.

Mr. Trump's speech ⁠in eastern Michigan on Sunday (October 25, 2026) came a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the State, underscoring its importance in ⁠next week's elections.

At a Saturday (October 24, 2026) rally in Detroit, Mr. Obama framed the attacks by Mr. El-Sayed's opponents as an attempt to make him look "less American than they are."

The former President compared them to his own experience as the target of false claims ‌that he was born in Kenya. "This stuff didn't work on me," Mr. Obama said. "Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."

Democrats need to gain just a handful of seats each in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives to overturn ​Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

#5515. Soldiers guard center of Milan as thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe

Members of right-wing student groups march through the streets of Rome, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a demonstration called "Unlock Everything," organized in opposition to recent left-wing student protests and one of several demonstrations held by groups across the political spectrum. Gregorio Borgia/AP hide caption

MILAN — Thousands of young people marched Saturday through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin, as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week.

The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin.

In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported.

Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported.

While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities Saturday from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.

Members of right-wing student groups march through the streets of Rome, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a demonstration called "Unlock Everything," organized in opposition to recent left-wing student protests and one of several demonstrations held by groups across the political spectrum. Gregorio Borgia/AP hide caption

The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing.

In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Meloni and holding aloft banners such as "No to lies of the state."

A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed.

The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence.

A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy Thursday, joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a center-left primary in early 2027. Milan's center-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again.

Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened.

Protesters march during a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Thibault Camus/AP hide caption

Rioters last weekend smashed their way into stores, targeting sneakers, athletic wear and sporting goods on streets that run off the city's central Duomo square.

Security measures extended beyond the city center over concerns protesters could move into other neighborhoods.

The protesters ended their march peacefully Saturday evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the city center.

Officials said Saturday they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the "mastermind" of the newly formed Oct. 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy.

Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them "naturalized, second-generation Italians," alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors.

A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police.

Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed Saturday were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorized to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said.

Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.

A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters.

"I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities," said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association.

A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.

But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organizers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and tear gas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about half a kilometer (mile) away.

In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets Saturday.

A protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Thibault Camus/AP hide caption

For over a week, protesters have hurled rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks at police who have used batons and tear gas in clashes in the city center.

High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama.

A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the prime minister's office turned violent earlier, with some activists lighting fires on the street.

Rama said Saturday his government was preparing a response to the students' demands and called them to a dialogue. He warned that violent protesters will face penalties.

Thousands of retirees and others marched peacefully in Spain's capital Saturday to demand public pensions aren't meddled with.

"They are threatening us with privatizing pensions. It's just another thing they want to profit from," said Maria José Benito, 68.

The protests came ahead of next month's snap election as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party criticized the conservative opposition Popular Party for making overtures about privatizing public pensions. Spain also has been roiled by protests this fall around the issue of housing, as rental and home costs have risen in recent years beyond what many Spaniards can afford.

Taking their cue from Spaniards, protesters in Lisbon demanding affordable housing marched across the city on Saturday.

They have also targeted recent measures announced by the government of Prime Minister Luis Montenegro that include easing the cap on yearly rent increases and facilitating the eviction of tenants who fail to pay rent.

Montenegro defends the measures, saying that they aim at reinforcing trust between tenants and landlords and boosting the rentals market. Protesters claim that the measures are not balanced and put tenants in a more vulnerable position.
