#5548. Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past

Actor Tiger Shroff, who made his debut in 2014, is known for his action roles

On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor.

Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt.

Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.

Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.

The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.

Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.

The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.

During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.

Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?

Watch: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting attempt in Mumbai

Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.

D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.

In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.

Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.

Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.

But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad.

"This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."

Gangster Lawrence Bishnoi has been locked up in prison since 2015

That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.

Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.

Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.

Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."

Bishnoi's gang claimed responsibility for killing Baba Siddiqui (right) in 2024, citing his ties to Salman Khan (left)

The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.

In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, while Manoj Bajpayee's portrayal of gangster Bhiku Mhatre in Satya became, in the words of film scholar Ashvin Immanuel Devasundaram, "mythologised and talismanic".

The fear and fascination of that era were "seared into the collective consciousness", Devasundaram told the BBC.

Each new attack brings those memories back, he added. But today's gangsters no longer need cinema to build their mythology. Social media allows them to shape their own image, circulating threats, claims of responsibility and carefully staged photographs to audiences far beyond Mumbai.

After the latest shooting, police reportedly stepped up security outside the homes of Khan and Rohit Shetty. The All Indian Cine Workers Association demanded greater protection, asking: "Today it is Tiger Shroff. Who is next?"

There is little evidence so far that criminal networks have regained their former influence over Bollywood's finances and decisions. But the latest attacks have exposed a different vulnerability.

Gangsters may no longer need to control an industry to unsettle it. A single shooting attempt, amplified across millions of phone screens, can spread fear far beyond its intended target.

Sivanandhan, who spent years confronting Mumbai's gangsters, knows the limits of even the tightest security.

"There is always a crack in the armour," he said.

#5551. Черное море стало самым смертоносным морским маршрутом в мире

Черное море признали самым смертоносным морским маршрутом во всем мире. Статистику привела газета Financial Times (FT).

По данным издания, с начала года более 570 судов подверглись атакам в Черном море. Жертвами ударов стали не менее 40 моряков торгового флота — этот показатель больше, чем в Ормузском проливе, где подтвердили случаи с 24 погибшими.

Удары затронули корабли у берегов Румынии и Болгарии. Из-за страхования военных рисков, которое может достигать 15 процентов от стоимости самих судов, владельцы начали отправлять в опасные зоны более старые корабли.

В августе 2026 года экспорт украинской аграрной продукции по морю снизился на 75 процентов в сравнении с уровнем поставок до конфликта. Аналитики предупреждают, что в случае, если перебои продолжатся, фермерам, вероятно, не хватит денег для весенней посевной.

Ранее стало известно, что Украина потеряла около шести миллиардов долларов от простоя портов Большой Одессы, который длится свыше трех месяцев. Уточняется, что экспорт металлургической продукции в октябре прекратился полностью.

Published - October 26, 2026 08:43 am IST - Rio de Janeiro

Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro arrives at his election night event after the presidential runoff in Brasilia, Brazil, Sunday, October 25, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, was reelected on Sunday (October 25, 2026) in a result that provides relief to critics of widening U.S. influence in Latin America.

With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon-to-be 81-year-old Mr. Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes — 51.8% of the total vote — over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro. The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

Late Sunday (October 25, 2026), Mr. Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, calling the move to extend voting hours unprecedented — though both he and Mr. Lula made the request — and asked for the election results to be annulled, saying they were impossible to accept.

Mr. Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-centre presidential candidates allied with Mr. Trump have been winning. Mr. Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-centre leaders. It also positions Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, to remain independent of the U.S., despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Mr. Trump.

A video published by Mr. Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with First Lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court.

Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.

In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the colour of Mr. Lula’s supporters — shouted “You lost! Cry harder!” to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Mr. Bolsonaro's signature colours. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.

Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Mr. Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Mr. Bolsonaro bested Mr. Lula.

“I don't understand how people can vote for Mr. Lula,” he said. “The country is collapsing.”

Mr. Bolsonaro had yet to respond to Mr. Lula's apparent victory, which, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as President. The next term begins on January 5, 2027.

The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Mr. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favour the incumbent. Mr. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favoured.

In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.

The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Mr. Zanin, who made the decision, is Mr. Lula's former lawyer.

Mr. Bolsonaro bested Mr. Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday (October 25, 2026) night's apparent victory by Mr. Lula marked the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency.

Mr. Lula faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Mr. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs while Mr. Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives.

Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Mr. Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Mr. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

This will likely be the last victory of the veteran leader's political career. Mr. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.

Ms. Rousseff was impeached for accounting manoeuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Mr. Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.

Mr. Lula was released from prison after 580 days and Brazil's Supreme Court annulled his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.

Since he lost the first round, Mr. Lula reorganised his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration, and boosted several government initiatives.

He joins Mr. Trump and Nicaragua's President Daniel Ortega — all aged 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.

#5555. Nearly 1,000 arrested across France as police find potential weapons on protesters: officials

Police in Paris, France, were captured on video Saturday firing water cannons at protesters following a march. (Credit: Lena Pontrucher/Abaca for Fox News Digital)

Nearly 1,000 people were arrested Saturday as nationwide protests resumed, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told reporters.

The unrest has spread beyond France, with violent clashes breaking out in Rome and Albania's capital of Tiranë, where demonstrators set government buildings on fire.

President Donald Trump also weighed in Saturday, pointing to the turmoil in France as a warning about what he said could happen in the United States under left-wing leadership.

Earlier in the day, police officers preemptively searched protesters and arrested people suspected of carrying potential weapons, including fireworks and ball bearings, Reuters reported.

Nuñez did not specify where the arrests were made.

AMERICANS WARNED ABOUT PARIS TRAVEL AFTER VIOLENCE, LOOTING AND TEAR GAS-FILLED STREETS

Thousands of protesters march in the streets of Paris Saturday. (Thibault Camus/AP Photo)

In Paris, where police estimated 110,000 people marched, officers conducted more than 3,000 checks and arrested 65 people, the BBC reported.

The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in protests nationwide, while union organizers estimated attendance at 800,000. In Paris, union organizers put turnout at 250,000, compared with the police estimate of 110,000, according to CBS News.

"Violent individuals have no place in the marches," the Paris Police Department said in a social media post. "The objective is clear: to prevent troublemakers from joining the procession, and to ensure the safety of the demonstrators."

Central Paris resembled a city under lockdown as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts, museums closed and more than 20 metro stations suspended service.

FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT

A protester holding a French flag and a sign moves through tear gas during a protest in Lyon, France, Saturday. (Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo)

In other cities — including Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice — police have resorted to firing tear gas to break up unruly crowds, Reuters reported.

Also in Nice, police used a water cannon to disperse a group of demonstrators who refused to pull back. And in Marseille and Lyon, there have been clashes between police officers and hooded youths.

The unrest also reached Italy on Saturday, where police deployed a water cannon against protesters in Rome as demonstrations over rising living costs and war turned violent. Reuters footage showed riot police confronting demonstrators before a water cannon vehicle approached and sprayed water toward the crowd.

Violence was also reported in Turin and Bologna, where demonstrators confronted police, while protests in Milan remained largely peaceful, according to Reuters. Italian authorities increased security after widespread rioting and looting the previous weekend.

In Albania, riot police fired water cannons at protesters in Tirana, where some demonstrators set government buildings ablaze and threw projectiles at officers. High school and university students have been demanding lower tuition fees, greater investment in education and an end to corruption in the education system.

Some protesters have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama. Rama said Saturday that his government was preparing a response to students' demands and called for dialogue, while warning that violent protesters would face penalties, according to The Associated Press.

Trump pointed to the unrest in France while speaking to reporters Saturday after casting his early-voting ballot for the 2026 midterm elections in West Palm Beach, Florida. The president criticized the country's previous leadership and argued that similar unrest could unfold in the U.S. under left-wing leadership.

Police officers detain protesters during a demonstration in Strasbourg, France, Saturday. (Jean-Francois Badias/AP Photo)

"Just two years ago, we were laughed at. We were a stupid country. We were a country led by idiots and morons and bad people and radical left people. ... Just take a look at France because that's what they'd like to have for our country, and I don't let that happen."

Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed across France to clamp down on agitators and prevent the kind of unrest seen during recent demonstrations, when cars were torched and the city hall building in Limoges was set on fire.

Last weekend, more than 2,700 people were arrested during protests that later turned into riots and looting sprees.

The nationwide marches were meant to reflect broader dissatisfaction with the French government, with protesters taking to the streets to air a range of different grievances.

A man tries to extinguish a fire during clashes between protesters and police in Paris. (Emma Da Silva/AP Photo)

The protests began weeks earlier and were led by high school and university students.

They were frustrated with teacher shortages and poor conditions at schools, including overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated buildings.

The movement gained momentum when major labor unions joined the demonstrations, broadening the protests to include opposition to the government's austerity policies and concerns over wages, pensions and the overall cost of living.

#5558. Australian MP's condition improves after alleged car attack

Helen Haines had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack

The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable.

The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday.

In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there.

Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges.

The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape".

Shock and disbelief: How the attack on an Australian MP unfolded in a small rural town

Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.

His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.

Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.

Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines.

Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.

Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

Supporters of the electoral list "Student List - Students Win" attend a final campaign rally at Slavija Square in Belgrade, Serbia on October 22, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

The story so far: As Serbians go to polls on Sunday (October 26, 2026) in an election to the 250-member parliament, speculation and forecasts have converged on two entities. On one side is Aleksandar Vucic, a radical nationalist who has held power for more than 12 years moving from Prime Minister to President and heads the prominent Serbian Progressive Party (Srpska Napredna Stranka or SNS). On the other side stands a leaderless group of students, academics, and other professionals seeking to take down what it alleges to be a corrupt regime which opposition members and international groups have flagged for taking an authoritarian turn. While Mr. Vucic has dismissed the group as a tool of ‘foreign powers’ and appealed for Serbian unity ahead of the polls, the ‘Students Win’ movement draws encouragement from the mass dissatisfaction towards the government and the recent fall of Mr. Vucic’s ally Victor Orban in neighbouring Hungary and is driven by the momentum built with nearly 2 years of protests and campaigns.

While Mr. Vucic’s term, as Prime Minister from 2014 to 2017 followed by two terms as President, saw allegations of authoritarianism with widespread censorship and crackdowns on dissent, the immediate cause behind the students’ movement was the collapse of a concrete canopy of a railway station in the city of Novi Sad in November 2024 killing 16 people. Improper modifications and unsound construction were blamed for the incident along with allegations of severe corruption prompting protests around the country.

An escalation occurred weeks later when students and professors of the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in capital Belgrade were attacked during a demonstration allegedly by an SNS mob. Students and academics across the country came in solidarity with their peers after the physical assault on peaceful protesters and launched mass blockaded over the absence of proper police action against the attackers. Over the following months, the movement grew with protests, marches, and blockades as sporadic violence and police action on the protesters earned more supporters for the cause with over 3 lakh citizens taking to the streets in Belgrade in March 2025.

The movement put forward a set of six demands, including the publication of documents regarding the construction of Novi Sad station and action against assaulters of the Belgrade academics. The movement says authorities had made multiple promises to fulfil the demands but failed to follow through.

The lack of accountability from the elected representatives and executives led to the group entering electoral politics. While the movement had called for snap parliamentary protests during the protests in 2025, it was Mr. Vucic’s desire to hold on to power that ultimately led to the coming election. With just months to go in his second term as President, the head of the Serbian state, and the possibility for a third term denied by the constitution, Mr. Vucic called snap elections to the parliament in hopes of switching back to being the Prime Minister and heading the government in an equally powerful role.

The Students Win, however, is not contesting the election as a typical political party. The movement has always opted to keep distance from the traditional parties and claims to be a decentralised, leaderless system with democratic principles depending on plenums, consultations, debates, and votes for decision making. Election to the Serbian parliament is held in a single national constituency with a proportional representation system where contesting parties get seats allocated based on their vote share after laying out a list of 250 candidates.

Students Win has come up with the ‘Students List’ with 250 names for parliament drawn up from the plena with many lesser-known names and no clear Prime Ministerial candidate. The movement’s website lays open for any and all volunteers to take up any role they feel fit in the run up to the elections, with tasks including door-to-door canvassing, operating call centres, observing polling station, transporting campaign materials, and delivering food and water. It has also put forward an 11-point reform programme for the country which includes eradicating corruption and freeing the media among plans for the economy and healthcare.

The only poll published ahead of the election, by New Serbian Political Thought, gave the Students List a minor advantage with 44.5% votes in favour against 42.7% for Mr. Vucic’s SNS. However, analysts have expressed concerns over a leaderless party forming a government. Sympathisers of Mr. Vucic, meanwhile, have come down hard on the students’ movement, opting to delegitimise the support the group claims to have garnered with its intensive and personalised campaign by calling it baseless and questioning the political and administrative experience of the new entrant. Mr. Vucic has gone all guns blaring against the movement, terming it an attempt by nameless external actors to destabilise the country in a ‘foreign-funded coup’, doubling down on the claims towards the end of the election campaign.

“They tried to destroy our country on an external order”, he said at the final pre-election meeting in Belgrade on Thursday even while making a call for reconciliation to his political opponents. Opposition parties, however, have acknowledged the momentum generated by the movement, as some parties chose to stay away from the election while others put out a smaller list for polls.

With youth movements making a wave around the world, including in India, the outcome of the Serbian election will be keenly observed by optimistic youngsters and ruling powers alike. A victory for the Students List will open possibilities for movements that do not require a popular face that could end up becoming a personality cult. But the challenge for the group, if victorious, would be to keep its decentralised and democratic identity intact in a parliamentary system that requires fixed roles and the inevitable positions of power.

#5568. Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic

From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.

There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".

Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.

"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.

The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.

Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.

Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".

Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.

The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.

Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".

Container units were used to host some participants as organisers opted not to build a traditional athletes' village

Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.

In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.

Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.

"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.

"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."

Organisers acknowledged major challenges and said athletes from some delegations had been inconvenienced

As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.

GL Events had won the 63bn yen (Â£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.

A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.

Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.

But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".

"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.

Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.

"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.

GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.

Volunteers were told they could attend the closing ceremony for free, before an organiser said that decision hadn't been approved

Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.

It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.

Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.

But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.

"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."

While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.

Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.

Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

Brazil’s former President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, mononymously called Lula, on October 30 defeated incumbent Jair Bolsonaro marking a comeback and the end of a decade-long right wing rule.

On first glance, this should not be a surprise — Mr. Bolsonaro, a far-right politician, presided over a disastrous COVID-19 pandemic response in the country with nearly 700,000 registered deaths and an economy that is slowly bouncing back but is still ravaged by high inflation (as high as 11% recently). The Bolsonaro regime consistently downplayed the threat of the virus and was lax in implementing vaccination and lockdown strategies to combat the pandemic. To shore up his sagging popularity, the regime resuscitated a cash transfer scheme to the poor to tamp down the effects of high inflation, but has also increased the government’s gross debt to GDP ratio to a high 90%. Mr. Bolsonaro clearly does not enjoy the benefits of being an outsider to the establishment as he did in the 2018 elections. He has also got to reckon with the candidacy of Brazil’s most well known politician, Lula.

A former union leader who has come from humble origins, Lula served two terms as the head of State between 2003 and 2010, before demitting office to his successor Dilma Rousseff of the Workers’ Party (PT) that he helped found in 1980. As President, Lula led his country through a period of economic growth and utilised a period of high commodity prices in the international market to subsidise programmes such as Bolsa Familia that instituted conditional cash transfers for the poor and lifted an estimated 20 million people out of extreme poverty. Lula’s two-terms coincided with the pink tide — the rise of left-wing regimes in Latin America — and he served as one of the key leaders of initiatives for intra-continental cooperation besides a promoter of multilateral international organisations such as BRICS. By the time he demitted power, Lula’s personal popularity and that of his regime’s philosophy, Lulismo, remained high in Brazil.

Lula’s rule, however, was qualitatively different from the more radical socialist-oriented regimes in Venezuela, Ecuador and Bolivia. While his working class origins and leadership of a strong trade union in the late 1970s during the military dictatorship in Brazil firmly put him in the Left, his government utilised policies of conciliation and negotiation to advance welfare, and did not quite disturb the hold of the traditional Brazilian elite over institutions of power.

The 2000s saw the participation of more Brazilians in the polity and a greater democratisation but the PT’s strategy of negotiating with the elite in Brazil’s Congress and other institutions ensured that the corruption in the highest circles in the country remained intact, affecting even Lula’s party.

The controversial Car Wash scandal, which revealed systematic corruption in the way contracts were awarded by executives of the state-owned petroleum company Petrobras and implicated several politicians, administrators and businessmen, led to the fall of the Dilma Rousseff presidency by impeachment in 2014. Even if Ms. Rousseff was not directly implicated in the scandal, it resulted in the decline in popularity for the PT. Lula himself was arrested, convicted and was barred from participating in the 2018 presidential elections, but was released in 2019 after documents leaked by journalist Glenn Greenwald pointed to collusion by Judge Sergio Moro with the prosecution. Brazil’s Supreme Court ruled in March 2021 that justice was biased against him, resulting in the cases against him being annulled and allowing him to run for President again.

Tackling authoritarianism is not new to Lula, though. In a book that came out in 2020, author John D. French writes about how Lula rose from humble origins to become a machinist in the fast industrialising Sao Paulo region and later, a popular working class leader by mobilising industrial workers in massive strikes during the dictatorship in the late 1970s. Lula’s style has always been to utilise dialogue with political opponents without giving up on an ability to “stand up and fight, when needed .. [through] an additive and transformative politics of cunning executed by creating spaces of convergence through difference”. Lula emerged as one of the key politicians in the newly democratic Brazil of the late 1980s after having cut his teeth as a working class leader and a leader of a national trade union confederation. His style of leadership and an ability to speak to Brazil’s poor through a unique “vernacular discourse” was intact both as a trade unionist and a popular politician and the leader of the PT.

Once in power, he continued to use the strategy of dialogue but moderated the ideological impulses of the PT even as he embarked upon welfare programmes that benefited the party’s core base. Yet, the PT and Lula’s critics in the left spectrum in Brazil argue that the party’s strategy to utilise a policy of conciliation and negotiation with the traditional elite allowed it to pursue reforms without blowback but it also helped the fortunes of the richer sections in Brazil — particularly those in the agro-economy sector. They argue that this also paved the way for the parliamentary “coup” from the Right that led to the impeachment of Ms. Rousseff besides the corruption cases giving a fillip to the rise of the far-right led by Mr. Bolsonaro.

Mr. Bolsonaro has never hidden his support for the erstwhile military dictatorship and has also suggested, in Donald Trump-like fashion — to whom his personality and politics are likened to —, that a loss in the elections would only mean electoral fraud, suggesting to his supporters that he will not accept defeat. There is now fear among some Brazilians that Mr. Bolsonaro and his supporters might stage an insurrection in the likelihood of an electoral defeat.

Lula’s triumphs against Mr. Bolsonaro is a victory for political decency and social liberalism over far-right populism and crass political discourse in Latin America’s largest country. Lula has promised that if he comes to power, he would implement new welfare, ecological and infrastructure spending schemes based on Keynesianism. But it would be a struggle for him to negotiate with a truculent and more powerful Brazilian Congress than during the 2000s.

26 октября в мире отмечают Дeнь aмилoидoзa. Православные празднуют Принесение в Москву Иверской иконы Божией Матери и вспоминают преподобного Вениамина Печерского. День рождения отмечает актриса Мария Семкина. Подробнее о торжествах, приметах и знаменитых именинниках 26 октября — в материале «Ленты.ру».

Амилоидоз — группа заболеваний, вызванных накоплением аномальных белков, называемых амилоидными фибриллами. Чаще всего у пациентов с таким диагнозом поражаются сердце и почки, а продолжительность жизни без лечения составляет от полугода до четырех лет.

В 2021 году Альянс по борьбе с амилоидозом и несколько других организаций учредили день, который в настоящее время объединяет не менее 18 стран на четырех континентах. Главная цель — рассказать широкой общественности об этом заболевании, обсудить меры по ускорению диагностики и повышению качества лечения.

Согласно преданию, в IX веке Иверская икона хранилась у одной благочестивей вдовы, жившей близ города Никеи. Однажды к ней ворвались иконоборцы — один воин ударил копьем по образу Девы Марии, и тотчас из пораженного места потекла кровь. Напуганная женщина решила спасти святыню — она дала воинам денег, а образ опустила в море. Так, икона доплыла до Афона, где ее приняли иноки Иверского монастыря.

Позже образ прославился своими чудесами далеко за пределами обители. Так что патриарх Никон обратился в Иверский монастырь с просьбой прислать в Москву список. 13 октября 1648 года святыню торжественно встретили жители столицы.

В народном календаре 26 октября — день Агафона, или Банный день. В это время на Руси было принято приводить в порядок бани, топить их и париться.

Indian tech workers are facing growing uncertainty amid US immigration curbs

For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.

Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.

New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.

Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (Â£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.

"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.

Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.

A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.

BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.

Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.

But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.

Vice President JD Vance's remarks on H-1B workers added to concerns over US immigration policy

A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.

"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.

Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.

While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".

While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.

Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.

Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.

Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.

While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".

Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.

Indians dominate the US employment green card backlog

The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.

But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.

Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.

Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."

While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.

Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.

Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.

Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.

"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.

Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

Published - October 26, 2026 08:17 am IST - Madrid

A bus crash in the Barcelona area of Spain injured more than 80 people, local emergency services said on Sunday (October 25, 2026).

The Catalan medical emergency services said 83 people were injured, including seven people seriously, 18 less seriously and 58 with minor injuries, in the crash in Fogars de Monclús near Barcelona.

Spanish news agency EFE said the bus had veered off a narrow, winding road and fallen down a 20-metre (65-foot) embankment on Sunday (October 25) afternoon.

The exact circumstances of the crash were not immediately clear and were under investigation, EFE said. Emergency services said they deployed 23 ambulances and two medical helicopters to the scene, as well as three joint teams of firefighters and medical personnel and three psychological support teams.

Olga Pane, Health Minister of the Generalitat of Catalonia, said rescue crews were searching the area to determine whether there might be any more victims.

EFE reported that the fire service also dispatched specialist mountain rescue teams.

#5585. France on edge with 70,000 police deployed for unrest as authorities probe suspected terror attack near Paris

CEO of Argil AI Brivael Le Pogam discusses the widespread unrest, business damages and arrests ahead of upcoming demonstrations in Paris.

A suspected terrorist attack near Paris Friday added to tensions across France as the nation prepares for more potential violence Saturday.

Seventy thousand law enforcement officers, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will be deployed across France as President Emmanuel Macron’s government tries to ward off another weekend of violent protests.

"The strategy adopted for the coming days is to ban protests requested by individuals or groups with no legitimate authority," Macron said ahead of the weekend after canceling his planned trip to Nigeria and Senegal originally scheduled for next week.

"The rules are simple, and I think they're just common sense," Macron added. "The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days."

FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC'

Protesters marched through central Paris amid clashes, fires and heavy police deployment during nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs in Paris, France, Oct. 17, 2026 (Firas Abdullah/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law," he added, "but alternative routes will be proposed" to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

Adding to security concerns, a suspected terrorist attack occurred in the city of Trappes, west of Paris. A 39-year-old man was arrested by police after one person was killed and four others, including a 12-year-old girl, were wounded in what was originally said to be a "relatively random" shooting.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has since told local media, "The motive may be racist. The investigation is ongoing, but this is clearly a terrorist crime."

The AFP reported the suspect appeared to fire randomly from a vehicle, and the mayor told reporters the dead victim and at least one of the wounded were "of African origin."

Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."

FRANCE COULD FACE EVEN WORSE DESTRUCTION WITH SECOND WEEKEND OF PLANNED RIOTS, STATE DEPT WARNS

Riot police officers run across a street during protests in Paris, France, Oct. 17, 2026. (Bruno Camillo/Reuters)

Ahead of Saturday's protests and after acknowledging that police had "lost control" during last weekend's unrest, Nuñez, the interior minister, said his ministry is "ready for tomorrow. We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass."

Reuters reports that the Union Nationale des Étudiants de France, or UNEF, one of the nation’s oldest student unions, has said its planned rallies will go on as scheduled despite police rejecting their permit requests. Police have so far only approved a union demonstration in Paris, Reuters reported, while denying requests from UNEF and the "Yellow Vest" movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018.

Macron also took aim at those he says are behind the violence, saying, "Last Saturday, we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic."

Riot police stand together outside the Pitié-Salpêtrière hospital (13th arrondissement) in Paris on Thursday, Oct.22, 2026,  (Jan Schmidt-Whitley/Le Pictorium via Reuters)

Earlier this week, Fabian Vanhemelryck, secretary general of the Alliance Police Nationale union, said political figures deserved blame because of "those who excuse the inexcusable, justify violence and prefer to overwrite police officers rather than condemn those who attack them."

He also said the "state that abandons its police officers in the face of increasingly uninhibited violence, while demanding that they accept, remain(s) silent and continue(s) to hold the line."

Major French institutions, like the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, will be closed in anticipation of Saturday’s planned protests, and 24 Metro stations across Paris will be closed. A Ligue 1 soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais, scheduled for Sunday night at Parc des Princes in the capital, has also been postponed to Monday evening.

French President Emmanuel Macron, center, hosts an Interministerial Crisis Meeting at the Elysee Presidential Palace in Paris Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, the day after nationwide riots. (Ludovic Marin/Pool Photo via AP)

The NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints, scheduled for Sunday afternoon at Stade de France just north of central Paris, is still set to be played as scheduled, yet some weekend events around the game have been canceled.

The Stade de France is the same stadium that hosted an international soccer match between France and neighboring Germany during the Nov. 13, 2015 terror attacks.

Explosions were heard outside the stadium during the game that night, with then-French President François Hollande in attendance. Fans were held inside the stadium for hours while authorities dealt with the attacks unfolding around Paris that night.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

Updated - October 26, 2026 07:35 am IST - Belgrade

Supporters of the electoral list "Student List - Students Win" celebrate after Aleksandar Vucic, Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate, conceded defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Serbia's student-led movement declared victory in parliamentary elections Sunday (October 25, 2026) ending 14 years in power for Aleksandar Vucic's right-wing populist party.

The victory in the snap vote comes after nearly two years of anti-government protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.

The disaster has been widely blamed on corruption and triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

"Preliminary results show that students are convincingly leading in almost all polling stations," Radomir Saicic, a candidate for the Students' List, said in a speech at the movement's election HQ.

"Students won and with them also a hope that Serbia can be a country of justice, freedom and dignity."

Voters cast ballots in huge numbers on Sunday (October 25, 2026), with the country recording its highest parliamentary election turnout in more than three decades.

Mr. Vucic conceded defeat less than two hours after polls closed, triggering raucous scenes in the capital as supporters of the movement celebrated the defeat of a government they blamed for deep-rooted corruption.

"I feel incredible," student Mila Martic told AFP from the List's headquarters. "I feel as though I am finally living in a free country."

Thousands poured into the capital's streets to celebrate the victory, with passing cars honking, crowds chanting, and fireworks lighting up the skyline.

According to the country's election officials, nearly 65% of its 6.4 million registered voters had cast their ballots by 6:00 p.m. (1700 GMT), two hours before polls closed.

The figure surpassed the 1993 parliamentary election, when just over 61% voted.

During his speech to supporters, Mr. Vucic said preliminary figures suggested the student movement could win between 135 and 140 seats, handing it an outright majority in the 250-seat parliament.

The 56-year-old statesman, who has maintained close ties with Russia throughout his tenure, blamed foreign powers for the result.

"I want people to know, this was the validation of a revolution carried out with the direct support of various European countries and the U.S. deep state, the one that is also against President Trump," he said.

For nearly two years, students have staged rallies and marched across the Balkan nation to reach voters directly and counter the media machine of Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party.

Their protests have drawn huge crowds, a final pre-election rally in Belgrade on Thursday (October 22, 2026) attracting around 150,000 people, according to an independent protest monitor.

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar congratulated the Students' List on their victory.

"We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union," von der Leyen said on X.

Mr. Magyar said he had talked with the Students' List leaders and assured them of his country's support.

"I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle," Mr. Magyar said on X.

Mr. Vucic's defeat comes months after his close ally and Mr. Magyar's right-wing predecessor Viktor Orban also lost the elections.

"A two-year-long dream has come true," Mirjana Nikolic, a candidate on the Students' List, said shortly after the win was announced.

Most of the student list's 250 candidates are experts from fields including academia and the arts with little political experience.

The movement has a broad platform, centred on a pledge to fight corruption.

It evolved from demands for a transparent investigation into the Novi Sad tragedy into calls for an early election.

Despite pushing back against the movement for almost two years, Mr. Vucic, under mounting pressure, called the vote last month, citing "major turbulence on the domestic political scene".

The right-wing populist leader resigned the presidency to run for Prime Minister.

Domestic and international observers were monitoring the vote, with students mobilising large numbers of volunteers to oversee the process.

Nomani highlights how these groups use specialized handbooks to train rioters and amplify chaos.

Fox News Digital's "Who's Who in Chaos Inc." is a living database mapping the organizations, local chapters, international networks and funders organizing or amplifying major protest movements.

The directory identifies each group's mission, ideology, organizational role and documented protest activity, distinguishing direct organizers and participants from supporters and amplifiers.

The database will be continuously updated and organized by country as new organizations, chapters, coalitions and connections emerge, providing a running picture of how local protest movements connect to broader national and transnational networks.

Masked protesters hold a banner reading "Autonomous antifa" during a demonstration of high-school students as part of a nationwide protest movement over learning conditions in Lyon, France, on Oct. 6, 2026. (Olivier Chassignole/AFP via Getty Images)

Tens of thousands of secondary school students and their supporters march from Republic to Nation square on Oct. 6, 2026, in Paris, France. Nationwide student protests and violent school riots have disrupted over 700 secondary schools and led to roughly 5,000 arrests across France. What began in late September 2026 as peaceful blockades in the low-income Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis has rapidly escalated into a major public order crisis for President Emmanuel Macron's government. (Guy Smallman/Getty Images)

#5598. Billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Jio launches India's biggest share sale

The Jio Platforms IPO is expected to be the biggest in the country

India's second richest man Mukesh Ambani's digital and telecommunications venture is tapping public investors for the first time in what's expected to be the country's largest share sale.

Jio Platforms, a unit of conglomerate Reliance Industries Ltd, aims to raise 302bn rupees ($3.2bn; Â£2.8bn) in the initial public offering (IPO) of freshly issued shares from Wednesday.

The company will use the money to repay loans it took to build and expand its unit Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd, India's largest private-sector telecoms operator.

This is the second mega IPO in a month in India after the National Stock Exchange's $2.4bn-issue despite the weakness in the broader equity market.

Arun Kejriwal of Kejriwal Research and Investment Services told the BBC that while the share market has remained subdued, the IPO market has been flush with issues and has seen interest from institutions and retail investors driven by attractive valuations and interest in new and scalable technology businesses.

He said that IPOs are being priced to reflect lower valuations and price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios among listed companies, making them attractive. The P/E ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay for each unit of a company's earnings.

Jio Platforms is offering shares in the price band of 1,065 to 1,119 rupees in the issue that closes Friday.

The share issue comes as the Nifty 50, the NSE's benchmark index of 50 leading Indian companies, has fallen by over 12% this year.

According to a Reuters report, institutional investors on Monday placed bids worth $3.2bn, which is 30 times the shares exclusively reserved for them and offered ahead of the IPO opening.

The response from institutional investors aligns with analysts' view that investors will be drawn to the IPO for Jio's scale, network infrastructure and established customer relationships.

Centrum Institutional Research, part of an Indian brokerage, said in a note that "with strong network leadership, large scale infrastructure, and a deepening digital ecosystem, Jio is well positioned to sustain industry-leading growth over the medium-to-long term".

But analysts also flag that competition is likely to remain intense for the company with price wars and potential churn in customer base.

Recently, technology billionaire Elon Musk publicly took on the low-cost Reliance Jio declaring that his Starlink's satellite internet service will be priced affordably in India.

Musk criticised Ambani on social media platform X as his satellite internet company struggles to get a final approval for a commercial launch in India.

The criticisms escalated with Musk questioning if Ambani was the "real boss of India". Ambani or Reliance did not respond directly to the attacks.

The IPO roadshows were led by Ambani's twins Isha and Akash who hold key positions in Jio Platforms

Jio also faces regulatory uncertainty even as the federal government has emerged as the largest stakeholder in rival Vodafone Idea after it converted its dues into equity as part of a relief package.

Equity experts flag that Jio Platforms remains exposed to regulatory risks as the telecom sector remains subject to extensive government oversight in India.

Retail investors have long viewed Reliance group companies as wealth creators and looked forward to IPOs from the conglomerate.

Founder Dhirubhai Ambani famously referred to shareholders as part of the "Reliance family", a tradition that has continued and created a loyal retail investor base.

The Jio Platforms IPO is the group's first public offering in two decades and signals a transition in leadership to the next generation of Ambanis.

Investor roadshows were led by Jio Platforms Managing Director Akash Ambani and Reliance Retail Ventures Executive Director Isha Ambani, the twin children of Reliance Chairman Mukesh Ambani who stayed away from the investors and shareholders this time.

Published - October 26, 2026 07:24 am IST - BRASILIA

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva celebrates with his running mate Geraldo Alckmin after winning a fourth term in the presidential runoff in Brazil on October 25, 2026 | Photo Credit: AP

Brazil's economy has beaten expectations in recent years, but mounting debt and entrenched structural problems could complicate leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's fourth ​term, which begins in January.

Here are the five main economic challenges he faces:

Brazil’s public debt has surged ‌more than 10 percentage points during Mr. Lula’s current term to over 82% of GDP, ​driving up borrowing costs.

The root cause is years of rising mandatory spending, leaving under ⁠8% of the federal budget adjustable.

Mr. Lula has sent mixed fiscal signals, at times dismissing debt worries as “nonsense” while arguing that strong economic growth would fix the problem.

His team has pledged to keep the government's current budget rules, which cap spending ‌growth and set primary balance targets — revenues minus expenditures, excluding interest payments on public debt — and hinted at tightening them.

Hitting those targets will be harder given Mr. Lula’s promise to raise ‌the minimum wage faster than inflation, which also lifts pension costs, after already raising welfare benefits and promising ‌new ⁠spending.

Even with interest rates at 13.75%, Brazil’s annual inflation ⁠of 4.6% remains above the central bank's tolerance range of 1.5% to 4.5%.

The central bank delivered its fifth straight rate cut last month on growing signs of an economic slowdown, but markets expect inflation to remain above the official 3% target ​until as late as 2029.

Mr. Lula’s platform promises lower ‌interest rates through fiscal discipline that spares social programs, but most economists say rates will only fall faster if Brazil cuts spending, and it’s unclear how he will square the two.

A record nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million businesses are behind on debt payments, according ‌to credit bureau Serasa, as high interest rates bite.

That has fueled public dissatisfaction despite strong indicators ​such as record-low unemployment and wage growth outpacing inflation.

Mr. Lula plans a new round of debt relief, this time through discounted purchases of distressed household loans from banks, plus tax ⁠debt forgiveness for some small business owners. Analysts say such measures offer only temporary relief.

The government has also discussed with the central bank ways to rein in heavy use of easy but expensive credit, such ‌as credit cards and unsecured consumer loans, though it has not detailed any proposals.

Mr. Lula will likely struggle to push his economic agenda through Congress after voters elected the most conservative legislature since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s.

Although he defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s (October 25, 2026) runoff, Mr. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies are set to control both chambers.

Mr. Lula’s aides have signalled that he will keep pushing to curtail tax breaks, but lawmakers have repeatedly resisted measures that raise the effective tax burden.

During ‌his current term, Mr. Lula has struggled to name nominees and win Senate approval for them at key institutions, including the Supreme ​Court, central bank, securities regulator, and antitrust watchdog, and that is likely to be even more difficult ahead with the rightward shift of Congress.

Mr. Lula won congressional approval ⁠in 2023 for a sweeping overhaul of Brazil’s consumption taxes, and a new value-added tax is set to ⁠take effect in January.

With under three months to go, the government has still not disclosed the effective rate, which independent analysts estimate will be around 28%.

Fearing a backlash during the campaign, ‌the administration has also held off on sending Congress a bill to regulate a new tax on products considered harmful to health or the environment, such as cigarettes and alcohol.

That delay could ​push back revenue from the tax and has fuelled criticism of the government’s handling of tax policy.

#5606. Brazil’s rapid election count puts spotlight on voting security ahead of US midterms

Footage from a polling station in Rio de Janeiro showed electoral officials retrieving the voting results reports and disconnecting the machines after the first round of voting on Oct. 4, 2026. (Reuters)

SAO PAULO, Brazil— About 125 million Brazilians voted Oct. 4 on machines that print no paper ballots. Less than four hours after polls closed, the country knew its presidential election was headed to a runoff between conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro and leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

That process has been in place for over three decades, and Brazilians have become accustomed to its speed, simplicity, accuracy and routine. The system is robustly audited, completely disconnected from the Internet, and is the largest digital voting system deployed on the planet.

Eleven days before the U.S. midterms, Brazil’s system, analysts say, could offer Americans a more secure way to vote.

The system has been widely praised and was also mentioned in President Donald Trump’s 2025 executive order on elections, where he cited Brazil’s biometric voter identification as an example. Yet Brazil’s count runs partially on the kind of paperless machines that the president has vowed to scrap.

STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS

Election workers prepare and seal electronic voting machines ahead of the upcoming general elections in Brasilia, Brazil, on Sept. 23, 2026.  (Mateus Bonomi/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Over the years, Brazil merged federal, state and municipal databases into a digital voting record, whereby voter identity, eligibility and single ability to vote can (and usually must) be verified biometrically. Nearly 9 in 10 voters unlock the machines with a fingerprint.

Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, or TSE, which designs the machines and oversees elections, says there has been no proven fraud since their 1996 debut. The 499,248 machines used on Oct. 4 never connected to the internet. Their software was open to inspection by parties, universities and watchdogs for 11 months before being digitally signed and sealed in public. Last December, the Brazilian government invited a record 149 outsiders to try to break the system; evaluators concluded nothing they found could alter results or reveal how anyone voted.

An electronic voting machine at a Regional Electoral Court (TRE) facility in Brasilia, Brazil, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026.  (Ton Molina/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

On election day, randomly drawn machines are fed paper ballots on camera as federal auditors and foreign observers watch and specifically track results.

Meanwhile, at closing, every machine used at every polling station prints its tally, which is then posted in front of the polling place with a QR code, so anyone can check it against the national count. In an email to Fox News Digital, TSE said each file’s digital signature "confirms that the result was produced by the electronic voting machine registered for that polling station."

Karina Stange Calandrin, a political scientist and professor at Instituto Brasileiro de Mercado de Capitais (IBMEC), says the system combines three traits rarely found together: voting is electronic, votes hashed to voter eligibility are stored locally in the machine and tallying is automated.

"It is an extremely secure and safe system. The machines never connect to the Internet and even the central database system used to transmit tallied votes to TSE must match results issued physically and locally by each individual machine without human interference," she said. Corrupting it, she added, would require breaking the seal of each machine and installing software that wouldn’t match the TSE’s version, automatically disqualifying its tally — a scale of collusion so large that it "simply could not pass undetected."

COLOMBIA'S 'EL TIGRE' SECURES PRESIDENCY AS LEFTIST RIVAL FINALLY CONCEDES DEFEAT

Brazil's right-wing senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) gestures next to federal deputy and candidate for governor of Rio de Janeiro, Douglas Ruas (L) during a campaign rally on the eve of the general election, in Campo Grande neighborhood, in the western zone of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil on October 3, 2026. Brazilians go to the polls on Oct. 4, 2026. (Douglas SHINEIDR / AFP via Getty Images)

The machines passed their toughest political test in 2022, when former President Jair Bolsonaro, now serving a 27-year sentence for plotting to overturn his 2022 defeat, spent years attacking their credibility without evidence. Bolsonaro is presently serving time under house arrest.

This year, for the first time, a Bolsonaro appointee ran the TSE: Justice Kassio Nunes Marques. Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, finished first with 47% to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45%. The machines at the center of the senior Bolsonaro’s controversy may yet hand victory to his son.

Florencia Ferrer, CEO of e-stategiapublica, which has audited elections in 17 countries, has no doubt the Brazilian system is the most modern and secure in the world. "In India votes are electronic, but each voter gets a printed version of their vote to take home, which weakens voter safety and augments coercion rates," she says, adding that Estonia’s internet voting and the Philippines’ electronically tallied paper ballots carry their own risks.

An engineer from the University of São Paulo’s Polytechnic School who audited the machines in 2014, and declined to be named due to the sensitive nature of his work, agreed. "While no system is completely infallible... we have found no traces of tampering, wrong-doing or malicious intent," he told Fox News Digital.

Still, some defend higher scrutiny. Security researchers say a clean record is not proof enough, and the Carter Center said voters should at least see a printed version of their ballot deposited into a separate area of the machine; otherwise, results integrity rests on software alone. Germany’s top court ruled in 2009 that voters must be able to check their ballot without expert help, effectively barring a Brazilian-like system.

Brazil’s machine has traveled mostly on loan to countries in Latin America, Africa and Asia. Paraguay adopted it permanently in 2006, with machines that now print each individual vote.

Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (C) waves next to Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin (L) and to his candidate for São Paulo's governor, Fernando Haddad during a campaign rally on the eve of the general election, in São Paulo, Brazil on October 3, 2026. Brazilians go to the polls on Oct. 4, 2026,  (Luis Robayo/AFP Via Getty Images)

"It’s obvious Washington and the remainder of the U.S. are way behind both technology as well as security when it comes to polling on voting day," Ferrer said. U.S. elections are run in thousands of local jurisdictions under 50 sets of state rules and about 30% of 2024 ballots came by mail, which is slower to process. Brazil has one national election authority, compulsory voting and no mail-in ballots.

Brazilians will vote this coming Sunday on Oct. 25. The winner is expected to be known and certified in under five hours.

"The question is not whether Brazil has invented a perfect voting machine. No voting system is perfect. It is whether democracies can combine the speed and consistency of digital tabulation with independent verification, public scrutiny and rules that citizens across the political spectrum have reason to trust," Ferrer said.

Solly Boussidan is an international journalist covering Latin America for Fox News Digital. He has previously covered international affairs, war, finance and travel for several U.S. and international outlets. He is currently based in Brazil.
