Published - October 25, 2026 03:36 pm IST - Makueni(Kenya)

A bus collided with a truck on Kenya's main highway on Sunday (October 25, 2026), killing at least 22 people, police said.

The crash came three weeks after 17 people died in another accident along the same highway linking the capital, Nairobi, with the coastal city of Mombasa.

Several others were injured in the Sunday morning crash and were receiving treatment, police said. The passengers were reportedly returning from a funeral when the accident occurred.

Makueni County Commissioner Abdullahi Khalif said that the death toll could rise.

The circumstances surrounding the crash remain unclear. Speeding and poor road conditions have previously been cited as contributing factors in road accidents in Kenya.

Kenya's National Transport and Safety Authority said the stretch of the highway where the crash occurred is a designated “accident black spot” and that recommendations had been made to address safety concerns.

#5830. Владельцев старых спутниковых тарелок предостерегли от неожиданных трат

Старая спутниковая тарелка, которая ржавеет на балконе или стене дома, кажется совсем безобидной, но это не просто бытовой мусор, предупредил общественный деятель, эксперт по ЖКХ Дмитрий Бондарь. Комментарий он дал «Ленте.ру».

Эксперт предупредил, что старая спутниковая антенна может быть причиной экологических и правовых проблем. Он указал, что металлическое «зеркало» устройства состоит из стали или алюминия, а закрепленный на нем конвертер содержит ценные цветные металлы и электронные платы. При этом в России законодательно запрещено захоронение на свалках отходов, содержащих полезные компоненты, которые можно пустить во вторичный оборот, предупредил Бондарь.

«Поэтому выбрасывать антенну в обычный бак для бытовых отходов нельзя, так как это может повредить контейнер или прессующий механизм мусоровоза. За утилизацию крупногабаритного мусора в неположенном месте граждан могут оштрафовать. Продать или подарить старую антенну можно абсолютно легально, но здесь важно вспомнить условия ее приобретения. Если в свое время вы полностью выкупили комплект оборудования, то вы являетесь его полноправным собственником и имеете полное право продать его на сайте объявлений или отдать соседу», — отметил собеседник «Ленты.ру».

Юридические нюансы возникают в случаях, если оборудование было оформлено в рассрочку или аренду у оператора: до полной выплаты или расторжения договора передавать его другим лицам нельзя, сказал Бондарь. Также, по его словам, ограничения часто касаются смарт-карты доступа: по правилам большинства операторов она остается собственностью компании, поэтому перед продажей комплекта ее лучше извлечь. Если антенна пришла в негодность и надо от нее избавиться, самый правильный и экологичный путь — сдать ее на переработку, предложил эксперт.

Ранее дачникам назвали важные правила при закрытии участка на зиму. По словам эксперта по ЖКХ Дмитрия Бондаря, при консервации дачи важно перекрыть воду, очистить дымоход, убрать сухую траву, обесточить дом и оплатить коммунальные счета.

Updated - October 25, 2026 02:46 pm IST - Islamabad

Pakistan reopened a key border crossing with Iran to resume bilateral trade and cross-border movement after a week-long suspension that stranded freight vehicles, disrupted supplies and aggravated concerns over LPG shortage ahead of winter.

Trade operations resumed on Saturday (October 24, 2026) at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Balochistan's Gwadar district, with border officials allowing commercial consignments accompanied by consignment notes dated October 16 or earlier to cross, the Dawn newspaper reported.

Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, confirmed that the crossing, also known as Gate 250, has reopened.

"Pakistan has opened the border with Iran at Gabd-Rimdan... and allowed trucks and other vehicles to move toward Iran and Pakistan with import and export goods,” Mr. Kalmati said.

Welcoming the decision, he said the resumption of cross-border trade will bring immediate relief to traders and transporters stranded on both sides. He said the restored supply chain is expected to ease a nationwide LPG shortage and reduce soaring energy and food prices across Pakistan.

The reopening of the border comes days after Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir's visit to Iran earlier this week, during which he held talks with the Iranian leadership on bilateral relations and regional issues.

Pakistan's Commerce Ministry had closed the border and stopped cross-border movement on October 17. Though the Ministry did not specify a reason for the decision, the suspension was believed to be linked to security concerns.

The closure of the border had affected LPG supply in Pakistan, the demand for which rises with the onset of winter.

The suspension was followed by an attack on freight vehicles stranded near the Gabd-Rimdan crossing. On Thursday (October 22, 2026), unidentified gunmen targeted the parked trucks, setting dozens ablaze and damaging several others.

The reopening on Saturday (October 24, 2026) followed a review of the security situation by local administrators, who deployed additional forces to protect trade convoys.

Pakistan and Iran share a 909-km border that separates Iran's Sistan and Baluchestan province from Pakistan's Balochistan province. The border crossings serve as important routes for bilateral commerce and the movement of goods in the region.

Updated - October 25, 2026 01:57 pm IST - Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on October 9, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday (October 25, 2026) after a two-week closure following strikes from Yemen's Houthis on the Saudi capital, though the Iran-backed group warned of more to come.

The Flight Radar monitoring site showed a plane taking off from Riyadh airport early Sunday (October 25, 2026), heading to the Saudi city of Jeddah.

Saudi Arabia, along with Yemen's internationally recognised government that it backs, has faced a wave of Houthi attacks in recent weeks after a years-long truce broke down in the summer.

The fighting has shifted the focus of the wider U.S-Iran war and deepened a humanitarian disaster crippling Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries.

"Please be advised that Terminal (1) will be designated for domestic flights and Terminal (2) for international flights operated by national carriers at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, effective Sunday, October 25, 2026," King Khalid International Airport posted on X on Saturday (October 24, 2026).

The Houthis have carried out waves of strikes on Riyadh's airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target".

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said early Sunday (October 25, 2026) it had shot down two drones in the Riyadh area.

Published - October 25, 2026 01:19 pm IST - Belgrade

Supporters of the electoral list "Student List - Students Win" attend a final campaign rally at Slavija Square in Belgrade, Serbia. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Serbia votes on Sunday (October 25, 2026) in what is set to be its most fiercely contested parliamentary election in more than 14 years, as a student-led movement seeks to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic.

The snap vote is the culmination of nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people, a tragedy widely blamed on corruption.

The disaster triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

The Students' List, a selection of candidates backed by the largely leaderless movement, now poses the biggest challenge to Mr. Vucic's right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has dominated politics throughout its tenure.

Eighteen electoral lists are vying for seats in Serbia's 250-member Parliament, but polls suggest the contest is largely a choice between the ruling party and the student-backed list.

Several leading opposition parties have opted not to run, instead urging supporters to back the students.

An unusually high turnout is expected among Serbia's 6.4 million registered voters.

In the decades since Milosevic fell, when around 70% cast ballots to oust him, parliamentary turnout has declined, averaging just over 55% during SNS rule.

For nearly two years, students have staged rallies and marched across the Balkan nation to reach voters directly and counter the SNS's media machine.

Their protests have regularly drawn huge crowds, with a final pre-election rally in Belgrade on Thursday (October 22, 2026) drawing around 1,50,000 people to the streets, according to an independent protest monitor.

Serbian students step up crusade against corruption

Serbia's protesting students rally to mark 7 months since train station tragedy

Thousands rally in Belgrade against crackdown on student-led protests

Mr. Vucic has also campaigned nationwide, embracing citizens in villages and towns, while repeatedly accusing the student movement of plotting a foreign-funded coup.

"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our State. Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at his party's final rally in Belgrade.

Most of the Students' List's 250 candidates are experts from fields including academia and the arts, with little political experience.

The movement has a broad platform, centred on a pledge to fight corruption.

It evolved from demands for a transparent investigation into the Novi Sad tragedy into calls for an early election.

Against them is Mr. Vucic, the face of his party, who has tried to cultivate an image as an indispensable statesman, walking a diplomatic tightrope between the neighbouring European Union and his close ally Russia.

Amid mounting pressure, the 56-year-old called the snap vote last month, citing "major turbulence on the domestic political scene".

The right-wing populist leader cut short his second presidential term to run for Prime Minister.

Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for "free and fair elections" were lacking.

"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organisations said.

"It is supported by documented findings from independent Serbian organisations working in different fields."

Domestic and international observers will monitor the vote, with students mobilising large numbers of volunteers to oversee the process.

Polls in Serbia will open at 7:00 am (0600 GMT) and close at 8:00 pm.

Electoral authorities have ordered overseas polling to follow Serbian voting hours, forcing some voters to vote in the early hours.

In Chicago, home to one of the largest Serbian communities in the United States, polls will open at 1:00 am local time, prompting voters to announce "pyjama voting parties" on social media.

But many overseas voters face a bigger hurdle, with a limited number of polling stations forcing some to travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres to cast their ballots.

A French flag flies as protesters stand on the Marianne statue of the Place de la République during a demonstration against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement, joined by French high school and university students, teachers and parents demanding better school conditions and government action, as well as labour unions, workers, farmers and retirees, in France, on October 17, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

France is in turmoil. More than half a million people hit the streets on October 17, as protests swept across the country. As the administration greeted the protesters with a large deployment of riot police, peaceful demonstrations were engulfed by violence in many places. Arsonists set fire to the Lyon tourist office and burnt down the Limoges City Hall, a historic municipal building. Protesters stormed the townhall in Marseille and attacked the prefect’s residence in Bordeaux. In Paris’s Place de la Republique, protesting youth who clashed with the police torched vehicles and looted shops. Luxury retailers such as Louis Vuitton, Hermes, Dior and Galeries Lafayette suffered millions of dollars in losses as their stores were ransacked. Police arrested or detained more than 6,000 people, including hundreds of minors.

With the police outnumbered and unable to protect public and private property, several cities resorted to full or partial curfews. Government officials have blamed the unrest on “seditionists from far-left fringe groups”. They have accused La France Insoumise, or LFI (France Unbowed), the leftwing political party launched by veteran politician Jean-Luc Melenchon (75), of inciting the protests with the aim of extracting political mileage ahead of the presidential elections in April 2027.

A drone view of mud covered properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, on August 26, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Story so far: The United Nations’ climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has approved a $21.6 million pay out (approx. ₹205 crore) to the Nepal government to help with rebuilding, following the devastating floods in August.

Formally, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), was set up to help developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change respond to economic and non-economic losses, including from extreme weather and slow-onset events. It operates under the financial mechanism of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022, and its Governing Instrument was adopted at COP28 in 2023.

As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions. Its start-up allocation is $342 million with at least half of it reserved for small island developing States and least developed countries. Its first call for funding requests drew 176 requests from 119 countries worth about $2.8 billion (₹26,600 crore). In July the Board deferred decisions on those requests to December.

It is the first time the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country. The Board took the decision at its first “extraordinary meeting,” held virtually on October 22, 2026. It also agreed to pilot, during the start-up phase, an approach allowing Nepal to submit a request outside the closed submission window. Any further such submissions will need separate Board decisions, and the Secretariat will assess lessons for the Fund’s long-term model.

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche, that experts say is linked to climate changed from human-accelerated global warming, set off flooding along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. Nepal estimates economic losses of at least $2.69 billion and recovery needs of at least $4.71 billion. The decision comes weeks before COP31 opens in Turkiye.

The $21.6 million approved by the Board includes $1.6 million in oversight fees, which are paid to the organisations that implement projects to cover the cost of supervising how money is used. Nepal has been invited to submit a funding request, which the Board will consider at its tenth meeting in Manila in December. Money would be released only after that approval.

The Fund has not publicly said how much cash it holds beyond signed contributions, and disbursement depends on donors honouring pledges.

Since its creation at COP27, the Fund has had to show that pledges translate into money for affected countries. The United States, the largest historical emitter, had pledged $17.5 million under President Joe Biden. In January 2025, the Trump administration withdrew the US representatives from the Fund’s board which was part of the US’ larger exit out of the Paris Agreement. At the time, pledges stood at about $741 million.

Jawad Khalid, a climate finance specialist writing for the Lowy Institute, an independent Australian think tank, argued that the Fund “still operates like a conventional development fund” rather than an emergency mechanism. “Its single funding cycle runs eleven steps, from origination through technical review to board approval. The Fund is hosted by the World Bank, which serves as its interim trustee,” he wrote in a piece.

Ajay Mathur, a former Director General of the International Solar Alliance, called the step “landmark” in a media statement. He cautioned that the sum is less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction cost. He noted that cash would flow only after further project proposals are cleared, risking delays to relief.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said in a media statement that while the Fund “took a historic first step” it it “cannot be a one-off.” He said no country should have to wait seven weeks, through “historic letters and relentless pressure,” to unlock an emergency meeting, and called for a permanent rapid-response system that moves support “in days, not months.” He said developed countries insisted the decision must not set a precedent or prejudge the long-term model, adding: “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions.”

Others read the decision more positively. Raju Pandit Chhetri, the Least Developed Countries’ lead climate finance negotiator, said it showed countries could reach “swift, effective consensus” and set “a strong precedent.”

Gadi Eisenkot | Photo Credit: Illustration: Sreejith. R Kumar

Anti-Netanyahu politics — this lies at the heart of Gadi Eisenkot’s campaign for the coming Israeli elections. According to several opinion polls, the strategy appears to be working.

With Israel set to go the polls on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), Mr. Eisenkot’s year-old centrist party, Yashar (Hebrew for Straight), is projected to win 20 of 120 seats in parliament, putting it ahead of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud.

While Yashar’s emergence as a frontrunner is a recent phenomenon, Mr. Eisenkot, the man helming this change, is far from new. For much of the world and Israelis, he is known for articulating the ‘Dahiya doctrine’ — a military tactic which received international condemnation for advocating the use of disproportionate force in areas where militants are operating from — and as a critic of Mr. Netanyahu’s strategy just months after the October 7 Hamas attack in 2023.

During the campaign, he has posed himself not merely as a politician promising to end forever wars but as someone who resonates with Israelis fatigued by a prolonging conflict.

Mr. Eisenkot was born to Moroccan immigrants in Tiberias and spent most of his childhood in Eilat. With a working class background, he has portrayed himself as an everyday person to voters. If Mr. Eisenkot manages to win a parliamentary majority, he would be the first Mizrahi – Jews of West Asian or North African descent – to become the country’s Prime Minister.

His enlistment in the Golani Brigade, one of Israel Defense Forces’ premier infantry units, when he was 18, marked the beginning of his 41-year military career. After rising through the ranks of the brigade, he served as the Chief of Staff from 2015 to 2019.

The 66-year-old entered politics relatively late, joining Benny Gantz’s National Unity party in August 2022. Less than a week after the October 7 attack, he joined Mr. Netanyahu’s war cabinet. He quit eight months later, in June 2024, accusing the Prime Minister of lacking a clear strategy.

In September 2025, he founded Yashar with just six members. Since then, the party has garnered significant traction and presents itself as an alternative to long-established parties such as Likud.

Also read | Netanyahu’s rival vows to end Hamas rule within 18 months if elected

But Mr. Eisenkot’s campaign is not solely political. Having lost his 25-year-old son and two of his nephews to Israel’s war in Gaza, he carries the appeal of a common person in Israel who personally suffered the consequences of the wars the government is entangled in.

However, much of what the former army commander envisions comes with ousting Mr. Netanyahu. In an interview with The Times of Israel earlier this month, he said: “My goal is to defeat him [Netanyahu] outright in the election and bring about Netanyahu’s retirement from political life. I think that is where the healing of the State of Israel will begin. I do not hate him, and I am not seeking personal revenge. I just think he failed.”

He has accused Mr. Netanyahu of waging forever wars, weakening international support, endangering democracy, and not accepting any responsibility for the security failures that led to the October 7 Hamas attack.

In contrast, he has promised a clear strategy for military operations and a commission of inquiry into the October 7 security failure. On Palestine and how to deal with Hamas, however, there is little difference between Mr. Eisenkot and his political rival. He has vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza within 18 months of taking office, either by implementing U.S. President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan “from a position of strength” or through “creative operations” aimed at destroying Hamas’s military wing.

He has promised to root out “Jewish terrorists” in the West Bank and halt efforts to annex the Palestinian territory. But he is opposed to the two-state solution much like Mr. Netanyahu.

The electoral arithmetic remains one of his biggest obstacles, with neither bloc projected to secure a clear majority. He has shown little inclination to include Arab parties in a future coalition, preferring to work with more Zionist parties. Even if Yashar emerges as the largest party, Mr. Eisenkot would still struggle to secure the support of a majority of Knesset members to unseat Israel’s longest-serving Prime Minister.

#5888. Ле Пен заявила о планах изменить подход Франции к зарубежным конфликтам

Лидер парламентской фракции французской партии «Национальное объединение» Марин Ле Пен заявила, что в случае победы на президентских выборах не станет отправлять французских военных для участия в чужих конфликтах. Об этом политик рассказала на партийном конгрессе в Орлеане, передает РИА Новости.

По ее словам, Франция не должна направлять своих граждан на чужие войны.

Updated - October 25, 2026 11:34 am IST - Hebron, Palestinian Territories

An Israeli Army vehicle passes near the closed entrance of Hebron, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Israel said on Sunday (October 25, 2026) all land crossings with the West Bank will be closed on the day of next week's election, as it pledged a harder line on militancy after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers in the territory.

The announcement came a day after Israeli forces pushed into the occupied West Bank city of Hebron and displaced around 2,000 residents, with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying, "they will not be allowed to return... until we've finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron".

Hamas, while not claiming credit, hailed Friday's (October 23) killings at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city, in which attackers shot dead two Israeli soldiers and wounded three more.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to exact a heavy price for the attack just days before polls and said he was planning an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967.

The Israeli Army said that, from Sunday (October 25), Palestinians would "not be permitted to enter Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley for work", using terms many in Israel use to refer to the West Bank.

The Army also said it would enforce "a ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings throughout Election Day" on October 27, it added.

Israel's longest serving Prime Minister Netanyahu is facing a tight race for a new term in Tuesday's (October 27) polls, with his security-first reputation all but shattered by Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.

The Palestinian Authority, the semi-autonomous body that governs parts of the West Bank in cooperation with Israel, called for international pressure on Israel to protect residents affected by the military operation.

The Israeli Army said that over Friday (October 23) and Saturday (October 24), it operated in 40 areas throughout the territory, with locals reporting that soldiers announced evacuations over loudspeakers late at night.

Israeli forces said they "apprehended approximately 40 suspects, including terrorists affiliated with the Hamas and Islamic Jihad terrorist organisations".

In the Hebron neighbourhood of Ein Deir Baha, nestled between two hills, vacated buildings were marked by X's and the streets were deserted, save a pair of Israeli military vehicles.

Israeli flags were draped on a house on the slope apparently taken over by troops.

Higazi Shawer al-Tamimi, 70, a shopkeeper who plays a leadership role in the neighbourhood, said he was awakened at 1:00 a.m. by soldiers and a senior officer who said he had to leave.

"I asked them how long the evacuation would last. They said: 'Until further notice.'"

He told AFP he had only a short time to pack, adding that for some residents, getting out of the neighbourhood was an ordeal.

"For example, my wife's mother, who is 90 years old and lives in the area, had to be carried out because she is ill," he said.

Right-wing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position in the defence ministry overseeing civilian affairs in the West Bank, said he personally ordered "the immediate demolition of a row of illegal structures" following Friday's (October 23) shooting.

"Anyone who messes with us will quickly understand that he will pay a painful price," he wrote on X.

To Mr. Tamimi, the West Bank operation is only happening because Mr. Netanyahu wants to win the election on "the blood of the Palestinian people".

He said people were not going anywhere. "I have lived through all the stages of the occupation, and I will die here."

But Mr. Tamimi's brother, Khaled Shawer al-Tamimi, 68, said he and his son left after the evacuation order rang out.

"The Army was announcing through loudspeakers: 'Leave the area.' So we left."

He told AFP he was surprised to hear Friday's (October 23) assailants came from the neighbourhood, which he described as middle-class and law-abiding.

"We have never seen or even heard a single gunshot being fired," he said from his son's sitting room as children flitted about.

The Israeli military said the operation would last several days, but Mr. Netanyahu suggested bigger action was coming.

Updated - October 25, 2026 11:01 am IST - Kyiv

Elon Musk. File | Photo Credit: AP

Tech tycoon Elon Musk accused Ukraine on Saturday (October 25, 2026) of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people", after tension between Washington and Kyiv over disruptions to the SpaceX-made network crucial to the Ukrainian army's operations.

"Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people," Mr. Musk wrote in a post on X, but added that that loophole was closed last week.

"Starlink's terms have remained consistent as a civilian system, not a means of killing. Violation of those terms will result in end of service," he wrote in another post.

He added that Starlink remained "critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now. Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately."

While Mr. Musk has shifted his stance on Ukraine many times since Russia's invasion in 2022, he has insisted that any disruption was the responsibility of the U.S. government, not SpaceX.

Kyiv relies on the civilian Starlink satellite communications system and the military-grade Starshield version as it tries to defend itself from Russian missile and drone attacks.

"Monitoring systems are recording a recovery in the speed of Starlink/Starshield. We are registering a speed of more than 400 km/h, the connection is stable," Defence Minister Yevgeniy Khmara said in a statement on Saturday (October 24, 2026).

"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he added.

"Right now, the speed is what we need. The restoration began during the night," he said on social media.

"This is very important; it's significant for our frontline logistics, for protecting Ukraine" from rocket-powered drones, he stressed.

The satellite network has been at the centre of a row between Ukraine and the United States.

Mr. Zelenskyy had accused Washington of helping Russia by failing to warn Kyiv of incoming missile strikes and hobbling its military response by throttling Starlink's speed.

Mr. Khmara credited Mr. Zelenskyy's "firm stance" on the issue, judging that it was "bearing fruit".

Women take part in a protest under the slogan "Red Card for the Government" against the lack of changes to abortion laws, in Krakow, Poland, on October 22, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

The story so far: Hundreds of women gathered outside Polish Parliament (Sejm) in Warsaw on Thursday (October 22, 2026), braving heavy rain to demand access to free and legal abortion, as demonstrations spread across more than 20 cities in Poland. Signalling rejection of the government’s record, protesters raised pro-choice slogans in a show of anger at Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s failure to deliver on his promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws.

The demonstrations came just two days after the lower house, the Sejm, passed two bills seeking to ease the country’s restrictive abortion laws. The proposed changes seek to roll back some of the restrictions on the rights of abortion imposed under the previous government, but their passage into law remains uncertain, with President Karol Nawrocki expected to veto the measures.

Poland has some of the most restrictive abortion laws in Europe. Since 1993, abortions has been allowed in Catholic Poland only on specific grounds. The restrictions tightened in October 2020, when the country’s Constitutional Tribunal ruled that abortion on the grounds of severe foetal abnormalities was unconstitutional. The ruling came into force in January 2021, effectively establishing a near-total ban on abortion. Since then, and under the current law, legal abortion is when a pregnancy threatens the woman’s life or health, or when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, like rape or incest. In cases involving rape or incest, termination is permitted up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Abortion on request is not permitted in Poland, and women seeking such terminations outside the legal grounds face major barriers to accessing healthcare. The law also criminalises assistance in pursuing an unlawful abortion, with penalties of up to three years’ imprisonment. However, the woman undergoing the abortion is not criminally liable. The restrictions have prompted repeated nationwide protests, including demonstrations in 2016 and after the 2020 ruling, with activists accusing the authorities of curtailing reproductive rights and restricting access to abortion care.

When Mr. Tusk’s coalition, comprising parties ranging from the left to the centre-right, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to liberalise abortion laws. However, disagreements between the coalition’s more conservative and liberal factions stalled reform efforts, fuelling criticism that the government had failed to honour its electoral commitments.

The issue has now returned to the parliamentary agenda, a year ahead of the next parliamentary election. On October 20, the Sejm passed two bills seeking to ease abortion restrictions.

The first bill seeks to partially decriminalise abortion by removing criminal penlties for terminating a pregnancy with a woman’s consent outside the grounds currently permitted by law, as well as for helping or encouraging such an abortion. It also proposes protections from criminal liability for doctors, nurses and midwives who terminate a pregnancy to avert a threat to the woman’s life or health, or in circumstances involving a high probability of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities or an incurable condition threatening the foetus’s life.

The second bill seeks to restore abortion as a legal option when doctors identify a severe and irreversible foetal abnormality or an incurable condition threatening foetal viability. This would reverse the effect of the 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling, which removed foetal abnormalities as a legal ground for termination.

Both bills would need to clear further legislative and presidential hurdles before becoming law. Even if enacted, they would not legalise abortion on request and would leave Catholic Poland’s near-total ban unchanged. Protesters have dismissed the new measures, calling it token gestures rather than a genuine effort to reform the law, arguing that the government is seeking to demonstrate progress on an issue that could influence its prospects in 2027 parliamentary elections.

Abortion laws vary widely across European Union, with countries setting different gestational limits and conditions for access. While several countries permit abortion on request during the first trimester, others maintain restrictive legal frameworks.

France became the first country in the world to explicitly enshrine the freedom to have an abortion in its Constitution in 2024. Abortion is permitted on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy and is covered by the public healthcare system. In Sweden, abortion is permitted on request up to 18 weeks, with medical abortions available at home under approved arrangements and costs covered by the state healthcare system. The Netherlands permits abortion until the foetus is considered capable of surviving outside the womb, generally around 24 weeks in practice, subject to legal and medical requirements.

Spain permits abortion on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy, while Ireland allows it up to 12 weeks. Finland also permits abortion on request during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, following a reform that took effect in 2023. Portugal permits abortion on request up to 10 weeks.

Ireland legalised abortion following a referendum in 2018, while Spain’s 2023 reforms removed the requirement for parental consent for 17-year-olds seeking an abortion.

Malta has historically maintained one of the world’s most restrictive abortion laws, criminalising the procedure in almost all circumstances. Before 2023, doctors who performed an abortion to save a woman’s life could face up to four years in prison, while women could face up to three years. In 2023, the country introduced a narrow exception to the near-total ban, allowing doctors to terminate a pregnancy when a woman faces an immediate risk to her life or when her health is in grave jeopardy that could lead to death. In non-immediate cases, the decision must be confirmed by a panel of medical specialists. The reform did not legalise abortion on request

Updated - October 25, 2026 09:28 am IST - Milan

People attend a spontaneous demonstration against the rising cost of living, a week after protests ended in clashes and looting in northern cities, in Milan, Italy October 24, 2026 | Photo Credit: Reuters

Thousands of young people marched on Saturday (October 24, 2026) through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin, as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely-successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week.

The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin.

In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported.

Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported.

While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities on Saturday (October 24, 2026) from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.

The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing.

In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Ms. Meloni and holding aloft banners such as "No to lies of the State".

A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed.

The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence.

A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy on Thursday (October 22, 2026), joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a centre-left primary in early 2027. Milan's centre-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again.

Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened.

Rioters last weekend smashed their way into stores, targeting sneakers, athletic wear and sporting goods on streets that run off the city's central Duomo square.

Security measures extended beyond the city centre over concerns protesters could move into other neighbourhoods.

The protesters ended their march peacefully on Saturday (October 24, 2026) evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than three kilometres (two miles) from the city centre.

Officials said on Saturday (October 24, 2026) they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the "mastermind" of the newly-formed October 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy.

Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them "naturalised, second-generation Italians", alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors.

A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police.

Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed on Saturday (October 24, 2026) were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorised to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said.

Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.

A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters.

"I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities," said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association.

A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organisers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.

But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organisers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and tear gas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about half a kilometre away.

In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets on Saturday (October 24, 2026).

For over a week, protesters have hurled rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks at police who have used batons and tear gas in clashes in the city centre.

High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama.

A separate protest organised by the opposition outside the Prime Minister's office turned violent earlier, with some activists lighting fires on the street.

Mr. Rama said on Saturday (October 24, 2026) his government was preparing a response to the students' demands and called them to a dialogue. He warned that violent protesters will face penalties.

Thousands of retirees and others marched peacefully in Spain's capital on Saturday (October 24, 2026) to demand public pensions are not meddled with.

"They are threatening us with privatising pensions. It is just another thing they want to profit from," said Maria José Benito, 68.

The protests came ahead of next month's snap election as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party criticised the conservative opposition Popular Party for making overtures about privatising public pensions. Spain also has been roiled by protests this fall around the issue of housing, as rental and home costs have risen in recent years beyond what many Spaniards can afford.

Taking their cue from Spaniards, protesters in Lisbon demanding affordable housing marched across the city on Saturday (October 24, 2026).

They have also targeted recent measures announced by the government of Prime Minister Luis Montenegro that include easing the cap on yearly rent increases and facilitating the eviction of tenants who fail to pay rent.

Montenegro defends the measures, saying that they aim at reinforcing trust between tenants and landlords and boosting the rentals market. Protesters claim that the measures are not balanced and put tenants in a more vulnerable position.

Most of the immigrants targeted by federal authorities in California this week for alleged voter fraud had applied for U.S. citizenship and now face charges related to lying on forms or during interviews. Those charges could lead to years in prison and thwart their efforts to naturalise.

Amandeep Kaur, who is among those charged, has lived in the country for eight years and is in the process of becoming a naturalised U.S. citizen, said her husband, Kulwinder Singh.

Mr. Singh said she got her driver's license in 2024 but took the written test at the DMV in Hindi because she struggles with English. He doesn't know if she registered to vote then. He said she received and returned a ballot in 2024 but they both thought it was a registration form.

Now, he said his wife is distraught with the news that she may have done something illegal.

“All she does is cry. It's heartbreaking,” said Mr. Singh, who is a U.S. citizen.

One of them is José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, who applied for citizenship in October 2025 after living in the country for 40 years and spending his entire adult life as a legal permanent resident. The federal government has alleged in charging documents that he improperly claimed to be a citizen in 2007 when registering to vote, then later lied about it on his immigration paperwork. The government hasn't accused him of casting a ballot.

Bañuelos-Díaz told The Associated Press he had no idea he had registered to vote until he was arrested on Monday (October 19, 2026) outside his Los Angeles home, though he recalls getting a driver's license around 2007. In California, people are prompted to register to vote when applying for a driver's license.

“I have never voted because I know I can't vote,” he said. “If there was a mistake, they should have called me out right away, not 20 years later.”

He was released from custody after his arrest but faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

Federal authorities on Monday (October 19, 2026) charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents in California in a crackdown on people accused of illegally voting or registering to do so. As of Thursday (October 22, 2026) morning, the government had filed charging documents in 10 of the 28 cases, offering additional details about how authorities relied on voter registration data to pursue broader criminal charges around immigration status.

Most of the immigrants charged in California have lived in the country for at least five years, and some of them for decades. They could face deportation if they lied on their citizenship application.

Immigrants convicted of illegally voting in the United States face up to a year in prison. Those convicted of lying on applications to become American citizens face up to a decade.

The Justice Department said in a statement that six people would be charged with voting as a noncitizen, a misdemeanor. The 22 others were facing a combination of felony charges including lying on their naturalisation application during interviews or on voter registration forms.

In one case, Homeland Security agents arrested Pamele Arbues Line immediately following her October 15 naturalisation interview in San Diego.

In charging documents, the federal government said Ms. Line had allegedly registered to vote five times and had submitted ballots in several elections but said in her paperwork and in the interview that she had never voted or claimed to be a U.S. citizen. She later admitted to registering to vote while getting her driver's license renewed last year and said she voted once, according to the charging documents.

Ms. Line, who is from the Philippines, told authorities she thought she was a U.S. citizen because her mother had become naturalised after they moved to the United States more than four decades ago. But Ms. Line, now 56, was 19 at the time and not covered by her mother's citizenship, according to the government. She learned she was not a citizen in June when she went to get a renewed Social Security card, and she told agents she applied for naturalisation the same day, according to the documents.

She faces at least 10 years in prison if convicted of two charges.

The cases are part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

The Department of Justice has sued California for not complying with a request to verify the citizenship of roughly 20,000 registered voters it says may be noncitizens. California, which has more than 23 million registered voters, has argued the state complies with federal law and that the Trump administration's numbers are likely significantly inflated.

State election officials also noted once a ballot is mailed in, it is separated from any individual voter identification, making it impossible to separate based on the information provided by the federal government.

Beyond voting, the Trump administration has also ramped up immigration enforcement nationwide and slowed down the approval of naturalisation applications. Government data shows officials approved 58,000 naturalisation applications between April and June 2026, less than a quarter of the number approved in the same period in 2025, according to the data.

Immigrants can apply to become U.S. citizens after holding green cards for at least three years. They must answer extensive questions about activities related to voting, political activities and crime, pass background checks and a civics test and meet English language requirements.

The Department of Homeland Security did not say what initially drew attention to the immigrants charged but said in an email that the agency reviewed naturalisation and other records in its investigation. Some of the court documents in the cases describe a benefits fraud audit performed by Homeland Security in August that started the process of identifying those charged this week.

“The voting rights of American citizens must be protected,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement announcing the charges this week.

President Donald Trump, left, and first lady Melania Trump listen to a question from a reporter after casting their early-voting ballots for the 2026 midterm elections at the Palm Beach County Library in West Palm Beach, Fla., Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) | Photo Credit: Mark Schiefelbein

President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday (October 24, 2026), saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.

Also Read: Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ while campaigning for Democrats

Mr. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office together after the President spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Mr. Trump has been criticised in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots.

Asked if he voted the party line, Mr. Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said, “Very much so.”

Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Mr. Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.

Mr. Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

As for the war in Iran, he said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”

Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine.

In Florida, Mr. Trump has endorsed Republican Representative Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.

He has also campaigned for Republican Senator Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon.

Published - October 25, 2026 09:03 am IST - Rio de Janeiro

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate seeking re-election, waves a flag during a closing campaign rally ahead of the presidential runoff, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 24, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday (October 25, 2026) facing a stark choice — another four years under veteran leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, or a return to the right under Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.

It is the final electoral battle for Mr. Lula, who turns 81 next week and is hoping to pull off a dramatic turnaround after a shock second-place finish in the first round to the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Final polls showed the two candidates neck-and-neck.

Sunday's runoff will determine whether Brazil remains one of Latin America's few leftist nations or joins a regional swing to the right championed by U.S. President Donald Trump, who has not openly endorsed the son of his ally.

Mr. Lula, who is seeking a fourth term in office overall, has pitched himself as a bulwark against U.S. interference and democratic backsliding and promised to expand social protections.

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has vowed to crack down on crime and slash government spending, while handing Brazil to "the Lord Jesus Christ," with a message of change that won over Brazilians looking for something new.

"Enough is enough. We've had 16 years of this administration, and it's clear it didn't work. It's time for a change," said Joao Paulo, 37, at a rally in Belo Horizonte, referring roughly to the total period Mr. Lula's Workers' Party (PT) has governed Brazil.

Flavio Bolsonaro has pitched himself as more moderate than his firebrand father, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for an attempted coup bid after his 2022 election loss.

He has vowed that if elected, his first act will be to free Jair Bolsonaro, a deeply divisive figure in Brazil whose legacy loomed large over the campaign of his eldest son.

After the first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro," where protesters recalled the former President's chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest, and cuts to public programs.

Deforestation of the world's largest rainforest has hit its lowest level in four decades under Mr. Lula.

Yet, as the El Nino weather phenomenon fueled fires that have choked Amazonian cities with smoke in recent weeks, climate change barely featured in the campaign.

Mr. Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic comeback to office in 2022 elections after a massive corruption scandal that saw him jailed for over 18 months.

The charges, thrown out on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.

In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about a high cost of living and are fed up with crime.

Mr. Lula's famed social policies became a point of tension, as he expanded welfare programs during the campaign, while critics want the government to rein in spending.

"Even if people call it handouts, for us they were an enormous help. Because anyone who has ever gone hungry knows not to take these programs for granted," said Walter dos Santos, 56, who lives in northeastern Brazil, a bastion of support for the President, who hails from the same region.

After his first-round blow, Mr. Lula revamped his social media strategy, turning to video selfies and even buying his first cellphone.

A fierce social media battle drew in Meta, parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, which Mr. Lula's campaign accused of favouring his opponent with "algorithmic manipulation."

Meta has denied this, but acknowledged that some of Mr. Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.

Whoever wins, Brazil is facing a bruising aftermath to the election.

"If the left wins, it faces four years with a hostile Congress and threats of impeachment," said political analyst Thomas Traumann, referring to sweeping legislative gains by the right.

"If the far right wins, it will be a government of retribution, directed at the Supreme Court," hated by the right after its conviction of Jair Bolsonaro over the attempted coup.

Flavio Bolsonaro has said he will seek the impeachment of Supreme Court Judge Alexandre de Moraes, who led the case against his father.

Published - October 25, 2026 08:34 am IST - Dakar

The attacks hit the restive west African country’s Menaka region, where gunmen reportedly rode in on motorcycles and opened fire on camps mainly housing members of the Daoussahak community. | Photo Credit: AP

Mali's armed forces said on Saturday (October 24, 2026) that they had discovered 54 bodies after attacks on camps in northeastern Mali last weekend, upping the toll by six.

The attacks hit the restive west African country's Menaka region, where gunmen reportedly rode in on motorcycles and opened fire on camps mainly housing members of the Daoussahak community.

The Daoussahak community is where the armed Movement for the Salvation of Azawad (MSA) originated, a group aligned with Mali's ruling junta, according to security and community sources.

Following the attack, a patrol was launched in the area which "discovered fifty-four (54) lifeless bodies in a camp in Tagadayat", Mali's armed forces said.

Sources had previously indicated to AFP that at least 48 people had died.

The armed forces said that the victims were buried on site and that nine survivors were evacuated to the city of Menaka.

It added that testimonies indicated that the attack was carried out by the Islamic State group's Sahel branch.

The targeted camps lie about 50 kilometres (30 miles) from the town of Menaka, in or around the village of Tinabow and the Tagadayat area.

The armed forces said that patrols and security operations were continuing in the region.

A security source based in the city of Gao told AFP last week that the massacre occurred "in retaliation for military operations carried out in the area recently and for attacks by the MSA".

Mali has been plagued since 2012 by a security crisis involving jihadist fighters, separatist groups and criminal gangs.

An election billboard featuring Bulgarian presidential candidate and incumbent President Iliana Iotova and vice-presidential candidate Kiril Valchev ahead of the country's presidential election on October 25. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Bulgarians vote ⁠in presidential elections on Sunday (October 25, 2026) as Russia’s war in Ukraine spreads to the waters off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast.

Polls place acting President Iliana Iotova, ‌61, and ex-caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, as leaders in a race of 27 candidates.

While the presidency is ‌largely ceremonial, Sunday’s (October 25, 2026) vote has taken on added significance after ‌a ⁠series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s ⁠Black Sea coast that likely killed some two-dozen international seafarers.

The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the ​government to seek allied ‌assistance to bolster maritime security.

Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.

Both leading presidential candidates ‌condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.

Mr. Gyurov, ​who served as caretaker Prime Minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed ⁠support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.

“I want Bulgaria to have a voice ‌of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position,” he said at a rally on Thursday (October 22, 2026).

Ms. Iotova, formerly Vice President, became acting president in January after Mr. Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ‌ticket. Mr. Radev supports Ms. Iotova, and they both call for a diplomatic end ​to the war.

A victory for Ms. Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female President.

“My opponents argue that there ⁠must be a war of attrition.” she told a rally on Thursday (October 22, 2026). “The ⁠truth is, we are all the ones who are most exhausted.”

Polls by Alpha Research give Ms. Iotova 41% of ‌the vote and Mr. Gyurov 28%. If no candidate wins a majority, a runoff vote will be held on November 1.

Voting starts ​at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and polls close at 8 p.m.
